Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: When was the last time you had to confront someone about their behavior?
Answer: I was having a bad day yesterday, feeling claustrophobic, hermetic, resentful. I moved through my errands lost in my thoughts, with my head down. I was not feeling social. I got into an elevator and hit the button for the lobby. I noticed it was taking a long time - stopping more than usual. There were only three people in it, and no one was getting on or off. A man inside the elevator started getting really exasperated. “This thing! It’s taking forever! Why is this happening? I bet you it’s going to stop on every flipping floor!!” “Shhh” I said. “She’s going to hear you, and think that’s what you want her to do.” He stared at me as if I was completely insane (I can’t say that I blame him). “Lady” he says, glowering at me, “I do not have the power to get this elevator to do anything. I am a nobody.” I glare at him. He glares at me. “You are not a nobody” I say. The elevator door opens. We all step out. I walk out into the street, feel the sun on my face, inhale a big breath of fresh air. I feel someone run up behind me. “Lady, thank you for saying I am not a nobody” says the man. “No one has ever said that to me before.” (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you distinguish between healthy compromise and losing yourself in a relationship?
Answer: Losing myself: I am making decisions that make me feel like I am compromising myself. I feel taken advantage of, resentful, and like what I am doing is a form of self-betrayal. Healthy compromise: I am changing myself because through loving you I’ve realized these changes will make me a better person. It feels like what I am doing is akin to growth.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it okay to humiliate your kid if he or her messed up really bad? Giving humiliating punishment and/or saying things like you don’t deserve respect, you’re a bad character, etc.?
Answer: If a kid messes up really bad, what I want them to feel is that I love them - no matter what. That they are good, and that sometimes good people make mistakes. What I want is for them to know they can change. That there is nothing wrong with them. Humiliating a kid accomplishes the opposite of all this. Feeling humiliated makes me feel not that I did something wrong but that there is something wrong with me. Not that I did something bad but that I am a bad person. Humiliation makes me feel bad about myself, in a way that is hard to heal from. The kid should always feel safe, and loved, so they forever carry the knowledge they are worthy of love. Parents have very, very deep access to how kids perceive themselves. It’s like they write their original code. Don't cause the kind of damage they cannot recover from.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend is upset that I don’t want to meet his family after a year. They have said mean judgmental things about me and him. Am I wrong or is he?
Answer: If your boyfriend wants you to meet his family after a year of dating, he is right. If you don’t want to meet them because you feel wronged, you are right. But, how is this helpful? To me, the crux of the matter is not who is wrong or who is right but what you both want the outcome to be. I want a healthy relationship with my boyfriend. I want to play the long game. I want to make it easy for the people who love him to spend time with him. If I laser-focus on what I want, what are the actions I should take, and how can my boyfriend and I join forces to end up where we want to be?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is cheating bad if the other person never finds out?
Answer: Yesterday in a yoga class everyone was moving from boat pose to low boat - in non yoga terms, we were doing crunches. They were really hard so I began lengthening my time in low boat, keeping an eye on the teacher so she wouldn’t see me. Then I realized me skipping boat made no difference to her. It made no difference to anyone around me. I was the one who would take from this class exactly what I put into it. I am free to make to do lists during meditation or I can make an effort to remain present and no one will know. I can put earnest effort into the class or I can coast, and no one will know. You may think there is no relationship between yoga and infidelity but see, my self esteem and my self confidence are built by me being a witness to the things that I do. Every time I am not present for my relationship, every time I get away with another lie, every time no one finds out, I find out. When I cheat, the only person I am cheating is myself. I am the one who takes from relationships exactly what I put into them.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you tell a friend that you don't see them as a best friend even though they see you as one?
Answer: I see no advantage in telling someone I call a friend (and therefore someone I love) that they are second best, or third. What for? But, more to the point, it baffles me that we rank our friendships. Inside my heart my friends are not a straight line in decreasing (or increasing) order of importance. They are all so different, it’s almost like each one of them has the same place, in a different way. Friends are like songs, all excellent and just right for different moments; or like food, all delicious and perfect depending on the mood. You don’t have to pick a best friend. You don’t have to be a best friend. Just love people, and let them love you back. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I found out that my friend lied to me about something recently. What should I do? I want her to stop the lying. Should I tell her I know, or should I just put up with it?
Answer: Difficult conversations mean one thing: this relationship is worth my discomfort. It’s worth me scrambling over something really hard to get to something more honest and more solid. And also, I have a fundamental trust that we can survive this. Deciding the difficult conversation is not worth having is deciding the relationship is not worth the investment. But it doesn’t stop there. Every time I decide to have a difficult conversation, I choose the difficult path over the easy path, and I practice. As I practice, I get better, and become a person willing (and skilled at) the creation of better relationships. Of course, there is always the possibility that the relationship falls apart as a result of the difficult conversation. In the end, what remains are the relationships worth keeping. What falls away are the friendships held together by me pretending, by me holding back; held together by all the things that hurt me and that I decided not to talk about.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What should I do if I feel lost and never find myself?
Answer: Imagine you’ve embarked on a trip across unknown waters. Suddenly, you feel like you’ve lost your way. There you are, bobbing, feeling unmoored. What do you do? Dedicate yourself to the vessel. The vessel is you. Set aside where you are going. Focus on how you can be healthier. Focus on how you can be stronger. Focus on how you can be more confident. Focus on how you can be more at peace. Before you know it, you will go from lost to found, and what you need to do next will become clear. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I've been best friends with someone for over a decade but lately she's been acting insecure and it's exhausting me because she won't listen to me when I support her. What should I do?
Answer: When I feel crappy and insecure, I need different things. By needing different things I mean I define “support” differently. Most of the time I just want to be alone, going about my business and talking to my thoughts. In this case “support” is absence. Sometimes, I realize I want to be alone but would benefit from spending time with friends to get out of my head and gain a more realistic sense of proportion. In this case, “support” is company. Sometimes I want to talk things through and get another perspective. In this case, “support” is your point of view. Sometimes I want to talk things through and just feel heard. I feel invaded if someone tries to fix things for me. I mean, can’t you just listen? In this case, “support” is just your ear. Sometimes I really want to know. What would you do if you were me? In this case, “support” is advice. Or, in your opinion, is there something I am not seeing that I should be paying attention to? In this case, “support” is your awareness. I have a close friend who has been my friend for over a decade. Whenever either of us is feeling out of sorts and calls the other, we ask - what does “support” look like today? Do you want me to listen, or do you want advice? Do you want to be left alone, or do you want to go for a walk? Do you want to talk about it, or do you want to talk about other things? I think we exhaust each other less when we outright ask what it is the other needs, and what it is they expect from us.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend always tells me to change myself. He doesn’t like me like the way I am. Why?
Answer: I would love to know why other people do the things they do. Why do people ask us to change, when you cannot change another person? Why do they choose to be with us when they don't like us, when they can be with someone who more accurately fits the description of what they want? Who knows. Whenever I am frustrated at my inability to understand why someone is doing what they do, I turn the question back to me, since I cannot answer for others, but can answer for myself. Which would sound something like: Why am I spending any of my time with someone who does not like me the way I am?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My husband’s friend always acts like we've never met, what do I do?
Answer: Hello. You are a very important friend to my husband, and he tells me so much about you. He’s told me about the time the two of you started a band and used to play in your parent’s house. He told me about how he went through a terrible breakup and showed up at your place in the middle of the night and you let him crash on your couch. He says that when his dog died you were the only person who listened instead of asking him to cheer up. Come over for dinner next Sunday! I would love to hear what kind of a friend he has been to you. People have a harder time forgetting someone who remembers them.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you get out of a manipulative controlling friendship knowing you will lose all of your friends? (because he will convince my friends to stop being friends with me if I try to get out of the relationship like last time)?
Answer: Here is what has worked for me: First, (and this is really difficult and really tricky and really life-changing) I question my own thoughts. I know I am convinced I will lose all my friends, but is this a fact, or a belief? Learning how to defy my own thinking is a vital skill because my thoughts lie to me. They have me living in a world created by my anxiety. This world is not real. Second, I think through the situation I am in. Can someone truly convince other people to stop being friends with me? Really? And if so, are these the people I want close to me? And, do I want to live a prisoner of this friendship even one more day, when any day I can say “You will always matter a lot to me, but we have reached a point where our relationship is not healthy for either of us, and I wish you all the best”? And, perhaps most importantly: if I am in a relationship with a manipulative, controlling friend; and believe all my friends can be convinced to stop being my friends, what role did I play to be in the middle of all of this, and what is it that I need to be doing differently? There is a future out there for me without this manipulating, controlling friendship and without easily swayed friends. But, if I am not very clear on how I got here, I will step into that future and recreate the same situation with these friends, or with new ones, over and over again.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can I become a happy person in general without useless answers?
Answer: A good question gives context. Many people on Quora want to answer questions, but are limited by not knowing anything about the circumstances of the person asking the question. A good question is specific. Asking how you can become a happy person “in general” invites generic answers. A good question is neutral. Asking a question and then being dismissive about answers that have not yet been given is likely to have an effect on the very people you are trying to elicit help from. There are many paths to becoming a happier person: one of them is to ask better questions. Asking a better question is equal to developing the power to get what you need. The better the question, the more precise and actionable your answers will be.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the best quality a person can possess?
Answer: If I feel defensive I am not open to another person’s perspective. If I feel like I already know everything, I have no ability to learn. If I feel I have nothing new to do, I become stagnant. If I feel like nothing can ever change for the better, I feel hopeless, and apathetic. If I feel like I am the center of the world, I feel egocentric. If I am not aware of all my prejudices, I become biased. The antidote to all of these things is curiosity: remaining open, eager to listen, receptive to change, hungry to learn, filled with wonder. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Does it sound over anxious to tell the woman you just met a week ago that you can't wait to see her again?
Answer: To many women, a man saying “I can’t wait to see you again” sounds anxious or intense. To many women, saying “I can’t wait to see you again” sounds really wonderful. My hope is that if you feel like you can’t wait to see her again, and feel like saying it, you say it. If she is a good match for you, she will love to hear it. If she’s not a good match for you, what a great advantage it will be to know that early on.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I overcome the frightening fear of being extremely lonely by being at the top?
Answer: Instead of overcoming the fear that “it will be lonely at the top”, I think of the things I can do now to defy the possibility of being lonely at the top when I get there: What if starting now I begin by cultivating self-awareness to diminish the chances of my ego getting the best of me? What if I make my family (chosen or otherwise) my priority, so that I have really strong relationships? What if I prioritize my friendships? What if I create a community of people with a job similar to mine so we always have someone to go to for advice or to talk and compare notes? What if I find a council of mentors? What if I made it a point to become a mentor to others? And, finally, what if I recognize loneliness is inherent to the human condition and make it a point to learn something from it when it presents itself? Most of all, there is no reason why I should allow any adage to become my destiny. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Question: Can you share a little of your happiness with me?
Answer: Yes please! My next book is coming out in a few months and Dan Roam just sent me the very first sketch for the cover!

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I show a person, through actions, that I will not leave and that he can trust me?
Answer: To show a person I can be trusted, the first thing I need to do is work on myself. An inability to own my mistakes presents pretty shaky ground. Self-awareness and taking responsibility make for a more sturdy, more reliable person. I make it a point to follow through on what I say I am going to do. I practice listening. I recognize both of us as flawed. Not “I want my relationship to be perfect” but rather “I know we are not perfect and am interested and willing to work on this relationship.” We practice open communication. We learn to say what we mean as directly and clearly as possible. If something bothers either of us, we address it. Any time something bothers me and I think “this conversation is not worth having” I am disinvesting in my relationship. We need to establish boundaries, so we can approach our relationship without resentment and without feeling like we are being taken advantage of. These things only work if we are both building a relationship, both learning to count on one another. As I learn to trust myself, he learns to trust himself. As he learns to trust me, I learn to trust him. Finally, trust means “I can count on you” and it’s natural for this to take time.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What advice would you give someone who is new to Quora?
Answer: Use your downvote button. Downvote anything that impacts the quality of Quora. I downvote and report spam. I downvote and report (rather than answer) questions designed to shame, provoke or insult. If I feel indignant and want to answer something pithy, all I do is give the question more circulation. I downvote anything that generates poor content. (What is X in one word? Any yes/no question, any question that requires a one syllable answer, etc.) Use your upvote button. Upvote something well written. Upvote anything you think others should read. Not because you agree with it - upvote it because it's good. Use your share button. If something is good, make it available to more people. If you disagree with an answer, write your own. This is how readers get more than one point of view. Quora is a metaphor for life. You get more of whatever is getting your attention. Switching what you click on will change your feed. Be nice and be respectful. Being nice and respectful on Quora unlocks the secrets of the universe.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can someone differentiate between a person who has healthy self-confidence and a person who exhibits narcissistic traits, especially when both seem highly successful and self-assured?
Answer: Self confident people are self-aware, treat themselves and others with respect, and are full of empathy. There is an ease around self-confident people. they have nothing to prove so make space for others: they listen, are happy for the success or good fortune of the people around them, are compassionate, know how to set boundaries and are quick to own their mistakes. Narcissists take the air out of the room. They voraciously seek attention, fill every space with with their energy, have no boundaries, disregard the boundaries of others, feel resentful when anyone else does well, and refuse to acknowledge their mistakes, which often demands they twist the truth to accommodate their reality. There is constant tension around narcissists, because they only think about themselves and are only happy when others are doing their bidding. They are insatiable: what they want is everything. You can distinguish one from the other based on how you feel after you’ve spent time with them. A narcissist will leave you feeling exhausted, resentful, guilty and second-guessing yourself. A self-confident person will leave you feeling inspired.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What's the best comment you read on Quora today?
Answer: I deeply appreciate every thoughtful, grateful and complimentary message I get. Here is one from today: I don’t think anyone can possibly overestimate the impact kindness can have on somebody’s day.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it easier to control people than it is to understand them?
Answer: Attempting to control someone requires vigilance, coercion, manipulation, threats and intimidation. Anyone I attempt to control will ultimately do everything they can to distance themselves from me. Understanding another person means becoming aware of my own assumptions. It means setting myself aside, giving another person my attention, my presence. It means listening with all of myself. Understanding brings you closer. But, it doesn’t stop there. Working to understand another person results not only in me understanding one person better, but in understanding others better, starting with myself. Control is aggressive, toxic, relentless and destructive, and in the end it cannot be done. Understanding is loving, healthy, constructive and ever expanding. The more I practice, the better all my relationships become. Understanding is much easier and much more rewarding. Controlling is not only difficult - it destroys everything and accomplishes nothing.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What does it mean when someone is called an "asshole"?
Answer: It means this person: Has a personality that is heavy, burdensome. Is self-centered. Is entitled. Feels deserving. Is manipulative. Is condescending. Is disrespectful. Exhibits behavior that irritates people (or irritates people intentionally.)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why does my girlfriend treat me like shit even though I did everything to make her happy?
Answer: I wish I had answers for why people do the things they do and for why they treat us the way that they do. Unfortunately, it’s near impossible to find these answers - particularly hard if we have never met either of you. Every time I rage in frustration at how difficult it is to figure out another person, I turn the question back to me. In other words, I take a question that renders me powerless, and turn it back to me, to return to me the power I have lost. This would sound something like: why do I do everything possible to make happy someone who treats me like shit?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you think we can cultivate a deeper sense of empathy and understanding in our relationships?
Answer: To any degree, practice: Less moving through the motions of my life, more noticing how I react to others. Less expectations, more awareness. Less opinions, more pausing. Less being wrapped up in myself, more curiosity. Less believing I have to fix it, more listening. Less “I am right”, more open to more perspectives. Less “I already know” more beginner’s mind. Less snap judgements, more remaining receptive. Less assumptions, more questions.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Am I too young to decide I never want children? I’m 18. I have dreams and passions that I want to follow, and a small business I want to grow. I want to travel the world, meet people and see/experience most things.
Answer: You can follow your dreams and your passions and grow your small business. You can travel the world, meet people and see and experience as much as you want. AND, you can say “I don’t want children, but my gift to myself is the fact I don’t have to decide. I can leave every option open, because that is consistent with my desire to see and experience most things.” If, as you get older, you remain firm in your decision to never have kids, that’s fantastic. And if you change your mind, that’s fantastic. It’s your life. Open every door.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: If a loved one is depressed and doesn't want to talk with you, should you give them space or keep trying to reach out to them?
Answer: I offer a middle ground. If I am feeling depressed or like I don’t want to talk, a friend might call and leave a message, or text, or even slip a note under my door. Any form of a presence that does not require I talk to anyone or call anyone back. This way I have the space I am requesting - plus a regular reminder that someone out there cares, and that I am not alone.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My GF gets mad at me easily and she wants space for something that doesn't matter than much. What should I do?
Answer: Ugh. I hear you. People can be so sensitive. How annoying, for someone to get mad easily about things that don’t matter. Except. What if something small for me is big for him? What if something that doesn’t matter to me matters to him? I can shut down his attempts to communicate with me (wow you are so sensitive you get mad so easily at things that don’t matter) or I can get really curious. Can you tell me more about why this makes you mad? What about it is upsetting to you? Why does this matter to you? Talk to me. I want to listen. I want to understand. Maybe at the end of the conversation I can know him better, support what matters to him. Maybe in the end he feels regarded and heard, instead of dismissed, diminished. Maybe I can say - I didn’t see it at first but you know what? I love you, so it if matters to you, it matters to me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Can small steps lead to big changes?
Answer: Imagine for a moment that I stay up late every night. I drink, stumble home at sunrise, sleep most of the morning. I tell myself that I am young, I am having fun, and that later in life I might not have a chance to do what I am doing now. There is nothing wrong with being nocturnal, loving being awake when most people are sleeping. There is nothing wrong with being the first to greet the day. And, if I am awake at night, why can’t I sleep in the morning? One day, I wake up at the crack of noon and pour myself some coffee. I sit on my couch feeling run down. I am hit with a realization. My life is not where I want it to be. While my life is entertaining, it feels stagnant. Nights used to be fun and now they seem indistinguishable. Wait. The things I am choosing to do with my time are not amounting to anything. To review: up until now, no actual step has been taken. I have changed nothing, except for one thing that has only happened in the recesses of my brain: awareness. An awareness that if I want something, I have to do something every day to move towards what I want. What I do every day is not an activity thrown to the wind but an activity that adds up. That’s it. That’s the end of the story. But let me tell you. Awareness is so small it cannot be perceived by anyone but me. I don’t even know if I can technically call it a “step”. And yet, it changes everything.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My girlfriend has broken my heart for the third time. I think it's finally time I let her go, but a part of me wants to beg her and have one last time with her. What should I do?
Answer: Years ago, a friend was telling me about her relationship and the heartache she was putting herself through. “The truth is, he is emotionally unavailable and as a result is being thoughtless in his treatment of me”. I told her I thought she was an incredible person, kind and loving, and that I felt she deserved better than what she was describing. “It’s very interesting to me” she said. “That you are so clear about what you think I deserve, but that you cannot see that you too deserve it.” I understood that day that I needed to want for myself what I wanted for my friends: not just someone who didn’t break their heart, not just someone who was not careless, but someone they could build something with. Asking for someone that does not repeatedly break our heart is a low bar. So, what would you want your most beloved friend to do? Because, your most beloved friend is you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the best way to stop self-sabotaging yourself, and how do you even realize when you are doing it?
Answer: Self-sabotage means I am getting in my own way. To stop getting in my own way, the first step is to realize this is what I am doing. I can’t change what I am not aware of. Here is what self-sabotage looks like: What I want and what I do are at odds with each other I feel I don’t deserve good things I make up problems that are not really there I ruin good things that happen in my life: good relationships, good jobs, good health Here are some examples: I put myself down and fail to question my inner critic I must get everything perfect so if it’s not perfect it doesn’t get done I never ask for help, then wonder why I have to do it all on my own An absence of self-care (I am sleep deprived or hung over and wonder why I can’t pay attention in meetings) I procrastinate (leaving things for later is a very clear sign that something inside me is working against me) I commit to nothing, then wonder why I have nothing to show for my time My master plans result in me creating what I fear the most. For example, I leave good relationships before they can leave me. I give up on everything too early, unable to see that self-confidence comes from pushing through setbacks Substance abuse - anything I do that is not good for my health - drinking, smoking, drugs - is a form of self-sabotage How to stop: Get very clear on the life that I want Notice when I am the one creating all the obstacles (Am I leaving things for later? Am I not committing to what I said I was going to do? Am I saying I want to be healthy, and then displaying unhealthy behavior?) Determine what kind of help or support I might need, and getting it for myself.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What’s the strangest feeling you’ve ever had and what triggered it?
Answer: Anxiety makes me feel exhausted, yet restless; riddles me with obsessive, unwanted, hyper focused thoughts and yet I can’t concentrate; I feel hyper vigilant and like something terrible is going to happen, even though I cannot divine the future. I think anxiety is pretty strange, because nothing triggers it.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What happens when you break a plate?
Answer: When I was a kid and dropped something and broke it, I felt terrible for being careless, reckless, thoughtless, clumsy, inconsiderate, for breaking something important, a part of a set, a heirloom, something that meant something to someone. To this day when I break a plate it makes me teary-eyed. Dushka, I tell myself, you really need to be more careful - as if my act was an act of insolence, as if I was being uncouth. Not too long ago I was at a friend’s house and my friend’s daughter dropped a plate. It shattered, and I froze. My friend’s daughter looked startled by the noise. My friend walked over to her daughter and said “you dropped a plate, and it was an accident. Accidents happen to everyone! And a plate is just a thing - it doesn’t matter. Let’s very carefully pick this up and clean up and then we can start over. Sound good?” Then they together restored the kitchen to what it looked like before the plate incident. “See?” my friend said. “It’s all good!” What happens when you break a plate? Nothing. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some very bad pieces of life advice?
Answer: “If it’s not a heck yes, it’s a no”. What makes this advice bad is that it has no nuance - it sounds like it should be applied to everything, rather than something that can be useful, but maybe not useful all of the time. Not every decision is unwavering and unequivocal. Many are more complicated, or more subtle, or require a pause. Many resist the formula of an impulsive command. I’ve made many, many decisions based on a “heck yes!” feeling but I’ve also decided to pursue things that made me feel riddled by ambivalence, doubt and fear. Put another way, I cannot buy into the notion that everything I decide to do is binary. It’s normal to second guess, to not be sure, even to panic and wonder what on earth I am doing. If I only pursued things that made me feel a heck yes, I would have missed out on many things I was not certain about that ended up being spectacular. Growth tends to feel really uncomfortable (hence the advice about the imperative to leave your comfort zone), so sometimes even a “heck no” is worth looking into. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What should I do when someone tries to make me feel guilty?
Answer: Feeling guilty is my own emotions telling me that I am a bad person, that I am selfish, that I fell short. Making someone feel guilty is a form of manipulation. “I want you to do what I want you to do, and I am going to make you feel bad if you don’t.” My first line of defense is to defy my own feeling. Does saying no make me a bad person? Or is saying no a mark of self-care? My second line of defense is to pinpoint my fear. What scares me? Am I worried about disappointing the person who is asking me to do this? I am. But, disappointing others is necessary if we are to do right by ourselves. As hard as it is, disappointing others is inevitable - and healthy. Is the other person taking advantage of the fact that I feel bad, saying things like “I can’t believe you would do this”, “I thought you were better than this”? This is a reminder that the other person is looking out for their own interests, and not for me. It’s very important that I take care of myself. That I set boundaries so that others respect my limits. If what another person is asking me to do compromises my well being, I can say “this is making me feel really guilty, but just because I feel guilty does not mean I am a bad person. It’s normal for boundary setting to be uncomfortable, even painful, and hurray for me for standing up for what’s right for me.” I wish I could tell you disappointing others gets easier over time. The truth is, sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn’t. Let’s do it anyway.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it bad if I ignore a friend’s phone call because I’m reading and enjoying my book, but plan to call them back after I am finished with my reading time?
Answer: Phones make us feel like we have to be available to everyone all of the time. This “always available” mentality does not lead to stronger relationships. It leads to resentment, exhaustion and burnout. Our time belongs to us. I can work, or read, or go on a walk, or go to the park and get back to people as I can, not because I am ignoring anyone, but because I am managing my most precious resource in a way that serves my life.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I have been late for work a lot and now I've been suspended and asked to write an email to my boss explaining why I should be able to come back. What is the best approach? It’s a family owned business and they have been more than lenient already.
Answer: “I have been late for work a lot” is an expression of accountability. It’s not shifting the blame, it’s not feigning powerlessness. “They have been more than lenient” is an expression of awareness, and also responsibility. From what I can see, the best approach is the one you already have.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Can anxiety make you a stronger person?
Answer: Life is hard. Life is change. Life presents me every day with legitimate reasons to feel anxious. In other words, it’s very easy to attribute my anxiety to what I have going on in my life and sometimes it’s not that simple. If my anxiety is always present, regardless of what is happening to me; if there is no real correlation or proportion between what I am dealing with and an ever-present sense that I am not safe, then anxiety is likely to have a negative impact on my health, making me weaker rather than stronger. If my anxiety is more than I can manage, if what is happening to me and around me exceeds my ability to cope with it, If I am feeling suffocated by it, then it’s overwhelming me. It’s pulling me under. If my anxiety is making me uncomfortable, if it’s a natural way to feel in response to the things that are happening to me and around me, if I am figuring out, day my day, moment by moment, how to manage it all, what I am doing is becoming resilient - to life, and to how I respond to it.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I make her desperate for me?
Answer: There is so much “advice” about leaving another person wanting, wondering, guessing, yearning, longing for us, desperate. On the surface I guess it can sound appealing to have someone be obsessed with us - but, if we look beneath the surface, it puts us at a huge disadvantage. Despair is fertile ground for a toxic relationship: irrational, frantic, urgent, insecure, jealous, possessive - abusive. It’s not fertile ground for a healthy relationship: even keeled, balanced, good for me, good for us. A healthy relationship can only emerge from feeling safe. From going through every day ups and downs confirming this feeling at every turn. Things got hard, and they are still here. I am safe. If all I can do is wonder “am I going to lose him?” “is there something wrong with me?” “why has he not called me back?” “where is he?” then my relationship is imploding (and so am I - despair is exhausting.) If at every turn I can see this person is steady, a lighthouse, a rock, that makes for a healthy relationship that will last. A relationship is not supposed to make me feel hooked, helpless. Feeling hooked is not love. A relationship is supposed to make me feel strong, connected. We can grow together. If I aim to make someone desperate, I am paving the way for a toxic experience for everyone.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it okay to read books and write on paper, even though everyone insists we should use the Internet for everything?
Answer: Ah, “everyone”. Let me tell you about “everyone.” “Everyone” is abstract, judgmental, nosy, disrespectful, erratic, superficial, frivolous, irrational, irresponsible and completely subjective. “Everyone” is a fabrication. I, on the other hand, am concrete, certain, steady, and the sole owner of my life. While “everyone” is a fabrication, I am real. As such, I get to decide if it’s OK to read books and write on paper, along with many other decisions I would never relinquish to “everyone”, despite their insistence.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What should I do? This guy wants to date me. However, he is asking me what happened to the last few relationships that I had. I believe that’s none of his business.
Answer: To me, if someone asks me questions about me or my past what they are saying is: I am interested in you. I want to get to know you. I want to understand what makes you tick. They are also saying: I want to know if I am safe with you. Are you accountable? Do you take responsibility? Are you aware of your patterns? Or, do you place the blame on others? How self-aware are you? What have you learned from your past experiences? They are also saying: Are you open? Are you emotionally available? Do you want to share who you are, or will you shut me out? When someone who wants to date me asks me what happened to the last few relationships I had, I need to decide. Am I interested in this person? Right this very moment I am being given the chance to set the tone for our relationship. Do I want to let him in?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can we improve ourselves in our relationships?
Answer: Listen more. Defend less. Understand more. “Win” less. More steadiness. Less drama. More focus. Less distraction. More attention. Less multitasking. More openness. Less secrets. More conversations. Less skirting issues. More clarity. Less wishful thinking. More respect. Less dismissiveness. More dignity. Less carelessness. More boundaries. Less resentment.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the best way to impress?
Answer: No one wants to be impressed by other people. What we want is to feel seen and heard. Does this person know who I am? Do they know what I do? Do they see me? Being impressive is a lot more about listening and asking questions than it is about attempting to impress. Being impressive is about letting yourself be impressed. We learn that everyone is interesting and has stories worth telling. Bonus: this takes the pressure off wondering what we are supposed to do or say.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What's it like having an unusual name?
Answer: It’s like being endowed with an instant icebreaker. Dushka Zapata? Dushka? Zapata? What? What kind of a name is that? Do you know what Dushka means? Do you know who Zapata was? Are you related? Where are you from? Yes? Yes? Yes? Yep. It’s mine. Yes I do. Yes I do. That depends on who is asking. You’d never guess.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Do people want to be deceived?
Answer: I can’t speak for “people”. I can tell you that when I am being deceived, something doesn’t quite fit. I look at the situation I am in and it feels off, off kilter, off its axis, and I carry a sense of incongruity, like a mirror that is uneven and distorts the image that is available to me. Then the truth comes in and click. The sound things make when everything snaps together can be a relief, or can be life-altering, devastating, but it is beautiful nonetheless: the perfect, clean note, unsparing, implacable, fierce. Ah. Now I can see. There is nothing like the truth and no matter what it takes away, I much prefer it to its counterpart: deception is meek, spineless, unctuous, a coward.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Do you know what it feels like to want someone so much it hurts and then for them to not really show any interest in you?
Answer: Wanting someone who is not interested in me is so painful it’s made me lose my will to live. The times this has happened have been such a terrible experience that I embarked on a quest to learn how to diminish the chances of feeling this way again. What I learned is that if I am anxious or believe I am not good enough, there is something about another person not showing interest in me that gets me hooked. I become convinced I can “get them to love me”. I mean, if I could just “show them” that I am worth their attention, everything would be different. This never works. If I instead am secure in who I am, someone not being interested in me means they are just not the right person for me - and that’s OK. A person who is not interested in me becomes… not interesting. Feeling self-confident changes who I am attracted to. I invest time in people who feel about me the way I feel about them. I believe I deserve people who feel about me the way I feel about them, and I believe you do too.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How does a normal person act? What is an appropriate act? How can I make long lasting relationships? How do I stay in a healthy long lasting relationship?
Answer: There is no such thing as “normal”. “Normal” means standard, “normal” means common - and many things that are standard and common are not healthy. It’s normal to want a fairy tale relationship and healthy to know that relationships have ups and downs and will never be perfect. It’s normal to pride myself on being “low maintenance”, and healthy to be unapologetic about expressing what I want. It’s common to be a relationship with someone who acts very interested, then not interested, and to interpret this sudden lack of interest as something I did wrong. It’s healthy to say “you switching from interested to not interested is not a result of my shortcomings - because you can have shortcomings and still be loved.” It’s normal to be upset when someone does not read my mind. (How does he not know why I am hurt?) It’s healthy to speak my mind instead of expecting someone to read it. It’s normal to dislike being alone and healthy to enjoy spending time with myself. It’s normal to compromise myself in the name of a relationship and healthy to set boundaries to protect the limits of what I can give. It’s normal to be thrilled by a roller coaster relationship, to interpret it as “passionate” - it’s healthy to want someone I can count on. It’s healthy to find reliability sexy, and not nearly as common as it should be.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some examples of long-term goals in therapy and how can they be used to achieve short-term goals?
Answer: To me, a therapist is like a person with a powerful emotional shovel. What I want is for them to dig under the things I can’t reach, to help me make these things more accessible. Long term goals in therapy might sound like: I want to better understand why I’ve placed a lid on my own happiness. What are things I can do in the short term to allow myself to be happier, or at least less shut inside myself? I want to better understand why I intellectually know something that happened to me was not my fault, and yet I feel like I am a bad person. What can I do in the short term to be more self-compassionate? I want to better understand why this secret that I have kept for so long makes me feel like I will be shunned if I talk about it. I want to understand why I experience certain feelings just like I experience nightmares. For example: in a nightmare, I am absolutely terrified to arrive barefoot to my office. In real life it would be awkward, but it would not feel as life threatening as it does in the dream. Certain feelings make me feel terror, and if I pause and look at them, what I am afraid of is unfortunate but not a threat to my life. What can I do in the short term to integrate my terror and my pragmatism? Why am I operating at two levels all the time, such as knowing exactly what happened and not believing myself? How can I both be certain and doubt myself? Why do I feel like I am making a big deal out of nothing, like when someone else says to me “oh come on you are being too sensitive”? What can I do in the short term to support what I know is not nothing? How can reality shift less? What can I do in the short term to not gaslight myself? How can I stop deeply regretting standing up for myself? How can what I know to be true in my head reach my heart and the rest of me? And, to me, the central question to every therapist. How can things that hurt me make me stronger, better at adaptation, rather than smaller and scared? Life is really hard, and I want your help to make me better at it. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can I get him to talk to me about the way he feels about me?
Answer: Hi. I am very keen on having a conversation about how we feel about each other. I know it can be uncomfortable and maybe even nerve wracking, so I will go first. I really like you. I want to get to know you better. And I am not interested in seeing other people. Can you tell me how you feel? I want to know if we are on the same page and want the same things.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can you play the game of a manipulative person?
Answer: Nah, look. Playing this game leaves me feeling exhausted. Like there is something wrong with me. Like I am powerless. Like there is no way for me to win. Instead, I step away. I do not participate. I do not react. I regard what is happening without feeling crushed, or blamed, or pressured, or accused, or shut out, or threatened. With perspective, I see things for what they are: not worth it. Playing the game of a manipulative person is not interesting to me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How much should we trust our feelings?
Answer: I trust the lilt and effervescence of my happiness 100%. I trust the bleakness in my melancholy and the fire of my anger and the disquiet of my regret. I trust the resistance of my fear and the painful spaciousness of my loneliness. In equal measure I trust all these feelings to be cursory, short-lived. Feelings are impermanent, so I both trust them and trust they will leave.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I make up relationship problems in my head and then imagine ways to solve them while thinking about my thinking. Is this a good thing?
Answer: You think you wrote this question but you didn’t. Your anxiety did. Anxiety believes that problems can be solved by imagining them, then working on them. It sure sounds logical, doesn’t it? Except, there is no limit to how many problems I can imagine. There is no limit to how much time I can spend working them. So, the exercise consumes me, and generates more anxiety. What am I overseeing? What am I not doing? You’d think that on the other side of all this I would at least end up more prepared, but I don’t. I just end up more anxious, frazzled, hopeless, burned out. Because it does me no good, what I try instead is to be present in what actually exists. If things are good, I don’t want to miss out on them in the name of imagining scenarios that are not taking place. If things are bad I want to be there so I can figure out how to overcome them. Then, I witness how I solve problems when they arrive. I learn to believe in myself and in my own ability to solve what comes my way. Self confidence and self trust are sturdier than anxiety, who is insatiable and cannot stop conjuring hypothetical, often improbable, increasingly unsolvable things.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why would a dad get angry at his adult son and call him out for posting an inappropriate and crude picture or post on Instagram when the adult son was only kidding?
Answer: “I was only kidding” refers to intent. I was trying to be funny and lighthearted and made a joke. I didn’t mean to hurt you. Posting something inappropriate and crude on Instagram might make someone feel exposed, invaded, even betrayed. Aside from feelings, posting something in a public place can hurt someone’s reputation. Once posted, it’s near impossible to delete. Posts have lasting consequences. This refers to impact. If someone is angry with me, and my response is “I was only kidding”, I am doing two things. The first is I am confusing intent with impact. Intent is all about me. Impact is about the person I hurt. To grasp why someone might be angry, I need to be able to see beyond my own perspective. The second is I am invalidating what the person is trying to tell me. If they are hurt, or angry, and I say I was only kidding, I am not listening. I am diminishing their experience. I am showing them that instead of saying “I am so sorry I hurt you, what I did was careless and I will do everything I can to undo it” I am brushing their feelings off as inconsequential. Understanding the difference between intent and impact and learning how to see other perspectives aside from my own will improve all my relationships.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My bf treats me bad and thinks that nothing he does is wrong. How do I make him realize he can't treat me that way?
Answer: I wish I had the ability to understand why people do the things they do. I wish I could adjust how they treat me, and to get them to see things the way I see them. Unfortunately, we cannot change other people. We can only change ourselves. To assist me in this effort, it helps me a lot to take all the questions I point at others, and point them back at me. Which would sound something like - why do I stay with someone who does not treat me well and who thinks nothing he does is wrong?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: When have you cheaply or inexpensively fixed an item someone thought unrepairable?
Answer: When I met my partner, I was through with love. In one of our first conversations I told him that I was happy being single (because I was), that it felt really peaceful (because it did) and that I was never really good at relationships anyway. Over time, I’ve accepted that it’s not that I’m not good at relationships but rather that relationships are messy. I learned to conceive of attention as a unit of love. Attention is what nurtures a relationship, and a lack of attention over time is what extinguishes it. I’ve learned that it’s important to fight well - rather than not fight at all - and to do so in the interest of each other, rather than in the interest of “winning”. I learned that commitment means “you keep coming back.” You keep coming back, even when things get hard. To more specifically answer your question, I thought I was unrepairable, and now we are an item. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are your favorite memories with your father?
Answer: I remember him sitting behind his desk in the library. I remember our long walks in the park, on the beach, around Central Park. I remember meals, and the flower market. The striped towel on the grass. I remember swimming in open water. I remember him sharing with me things he liked: a sip of wine, a bite of ravioli, a paragraph in the book he was reading (“Look, look how beautiful! You gotta read from here to here.”) But, what I remember most vividly is the sense that my arrival was something he celebrated. He lit up whenever he saw me, and that is my favorite memory of my father, and what he left imprinted in my heart.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What should you know before your first relationship?
Answer: Love yourself. Before you roll your eyes, hear me out. In relationships, how another person sees us tends to define us. Loving myself means I can put how another person sees me in perspective, so I have an ability to separate their opinion of me from who I really am. (For example, if you decide you no longer love me, this does not mean I am not worthy of love.) Represent yourself. When we are eager to be liked, it’s common to say what we think others want to hear, which keeps people from getting to know us. It’s important to learn how to express what I want, what I need, and what I like so the other person can get a sense for me, rather than who I am pretending to be. Respect yourself. Define what you value as important, take good care of yourself, don’t compare yourself to others, and know you deserve to be treated well. Pay attention. Consider your attention (giving it, or not giving it) a unit of love. Don’t abandon other parts of your life. It’s so common to want nothing more than to spend time with the person I am in a relationship with - this leads to me neglecting other relationships and other interests. It’s better for the health of the relationship to balance it out with other things. This includes spending time with myself. Love well. Tell the truth. Learn how to communicate. Do what you say you’re going to do. Learn how to give the best of you, by speaking up, by setting boundaries, by working towards being a safe space for the people who are important to you. Accept. No relationship is perfect. You are doing nothing wrong - humans are messy. Accept the mess rather than wondering why “you’re not doing it right.” Learn to fight. You don’t fight to hurt the other. You don’t fight to win. You fight to understand and be understood. There is no rush. When I am in love I want it all and I want it now and relationships have their own cadence. You cannot change another person. If you are hoping the other person will change, if you are spending time pushing, persuading, manipulating, nagging, you are just diverting energy that you need to expend on changing yourself. Most relationships end (which is normal, and not a sign of failure.) The fact they are ephemeral is all the more reason to give them the best of you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is one thing that is hard for you to get over when it comes to mistakes in the past year?
Answer: When I was a kid I felt very responsible for the emotional well being of others and spent a lot of time and energy making sure everyone was happy and getting along. It gave me a sense of purpose. It also made me sick. As an adult I can see how preposterous all this sounds. I’ve learned that this was never my job. Or, to put a finer point on it, I’ve learned intellectually that this is not my job and work every day at getting my systems updated to what I already know in my head but is harder to reconcile with my behavior. Today, I put a lot of thought into distinguishing what is and what is not up to me to manage, regulate, save or fix. I put a lot of thought into setting boundaries (a lot - I even wrote a book about it), and in having difficult conversations. Setting boundaries might sound like “this is the role I used to play in the past but I don’t want to play it this way anymore so I am not going to do that, even if refraining makes me really uncomfortable.” A difficult conversation might sound like “I can no longer keep the peace at the cost of compromising myself.” The reason I am changing my behavior is because my previous behavior was taking a toll on me and as such it was not sustainable. The consequences of changing my behavior have been, for the most part, fortunate. I think my relationships are better, deeper, healthier and more consistent with what I can do (rather than consistent with me overextending myself and living a life full of resentment and disbelief.) In a couple of cases, the consequences of me changing my behavior have been…catastrophic. They have left me wondering at an existential level if having difficult conversations was a mistake - if I would have been better off saying nothing and stewing silently, rather than being very open and expecting the relationship could withstand redesigning it. To get back to your question, the one thing that is hard for me to get over is this: if what you expect from me hurts me, and you are not willing to listen, to talk about it or attempt to see a perspective other than your own, did I make a mistake? Was I wrong to bring it up? And, if you don’t want me to, what recourse do I have to save us?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How much irrational information is necessary for conditioning and developing irrational decisions?
Answer: None. We can make irrational decisions without irrational information. We can even make irrational decisions with rational information. There is too much information to process so our brains take shortcuts. We accept probability as fact. We let our emotions guide us. We make mistakes and then make them again. We are impulsive. We look at what others do, even if we don’t like who they are or the lives they have. We like what is familiar and what feels safe (even if it isn’t.) We like comfort (even if it makes us unhappy.) We are not logical. It’s a wonder we ever make the right decision.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I lack motivation but want to succeed. What do I do?
Answer: Who needs motivation? That thing is erratic, mercurial and inconsistent. Instead, call on discipline. Call on grit. Call on this want you say you have, and make this want the decision maker. Define what success looks like for you and break it down into small increments. With those, create a routine you can follow through on every day. Make up for your lack of motivation with focus. You may not be motivated to do many things, but if you focus you can deliver on one thing, or two. Make it count.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Who am I really? What is reality anyways? Do I even matter? What is the point of this all?
Answer: One of my yoga teachers left today on maternity leave. I took her last class before her emotional departure, went over to hug her and said “you support me more than you will ever know.” To this she said “many times that I have doubted my path I turn around and see you sitting on the front row. YOU support me more than you will ever know.” This hit me hard. There are so many things we deliberately do to support others: assurance, assistance, attention and kindness. But there is so much we grant others just by being present, by trudging along, fighting our own battles. I can tell you for certain that you matter more than you will ever know, and that you save people from despair every day just by existing. This is reality, and the point is you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: The other day, my girlfriend got angry with me for not showing any interest in the book club she is a member of. Is it bad that I frankly don't care what goes on during her club's meetings?
Answer: My partner is an airplane fanatic. He can hear a plane and name it before seeing it. When he sees one, he can tell me which airplane it is and who designed it. With wide, shiny eyes he blurts out things like “this is a Spitfire. It was originally designed in 1937 by RJ Mitchell and became the most elegant, romantic and heroic flying machine of all time”. In his free time he makes model airplanes, sometimes assembling them and sometimes using a vacuform machine to make them from scratch. Alas. I don’t care about airplanes. I don’t ever pretend to be interested in something I am not interested in, but when he drops airplane tidbits what he is saying is “I love you and want to share with you something I love.” I mean, what an honor. I listen, ask a lot of questions, and do everything I can think of to support this passion of his. Whenever we visit a new city I check and see if they have an aviation museum and make sure we make the time to go. Do you know what I find incredible? That humans always dreamed of flying and that we did it. In 100 years, we went from “this cannot be done” to putting hundreds of people into machines that take us clear across the world while we sleep. Before the existence of my partner I had not given this any thought, and I am grateful to him for giving me the greatest gift of all time: awe. The single most steady, most reliable way to strengthen a relationship is to pay attention. Paying attention means “I care.” It means “I am not interested in what you are interested in, but I am interested in you.” Bonus: In giving someone your attention, you discover wondrous things. (Drawing by Dan Roam) Want to check out his model airplanes? They are amazing:

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My "boyfriend" never says its over instead he insults me and makes me believe he doesn't want me then later says we didn't break up. This is the last message, wouldn't this be considered a break up?
Answer: Alas. We don’t have conclusive answers to your relationship status. Perhaps more surprisingly, neither does your boyfriend. If someone does not say it’s over and instead insults me, if someone makes me believe he doesn’t want me, I get to decide what I consider this to be. It’s my relationship, I have free will, and no one can decide for me if I am or am not in a relationship. Instead of asking him if we are or are not broken up, I can instead ask myself why I am spending my time and my energy on someone who insults me and says he doesn’t want me. The one I need answers from is me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do I feel like I’ll never be able to change and if I do, it won’t last?
Answer: I have no way to know why you feel the way you do but here is what I do know: I don’t have to believe everything I feel. I can say “wow, look! I feel like I’ll never be able to change. Hello, feeling. You are lying to me. You think I am fixed, stagnant, passive, stuck; and instead I am revolution, transformation, metamorphosis.” I can talk to my feeling. Hey. Why are you lying? What is it that you are trying to keep us from doing? Maybe you want to keep us safe. Maybe you want us to stay within what we know, because familiar feels better than unknown. But, you know what? Change is survival. It is resilience. Change is life. I can defy my feeling. I know you think we can’t do this but I am going to show you that we can. I will be proof that you can be wrong. And then, I will stand as my own reminder that I can do things even when I believe that I can’t. And, that I can make these things enduring, lasting, sticky, perpetual. Go. Go show you what you can do.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I want to make myself more difficult to understand. How should I do it?
Answer: Not all communication is verbal. Your first step is to master looking at others with disdain. With contempt. Develop a withering look worth trademarking. Make sure people can see right away that they are in the presence of someone superior. At all costs, avoid listening. Speak without pausing. Speak without thinking. Make others conclude that what you are saying is not important and has no bearing on them or their life. Make others feel like you are attacking their character so they are too distraught and distracted to give you their attention. Use big words. Use the wrong words in the wrong places. Use a lot of industry jargon. Extra points if it includes acronyms. If you are not quite sure what you want to say, say more. Never get to the point. Don’t even have a point. If, alas, you happen to have a point, belabor it. Say one thing and mean another. Say one thing and do another. Make promises you do not deliver on. Say you would never do something and then go do it.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I am suffering from regret, feeling that I have had many missed opportunities in life and have made bad decisions. I feel like my life has been for nothing. I am suffering daily. How do I cope with this?
Answer: When I am dealing with regret, I take a notebook and write out everything I can about what it is that I am regretting. If there is something I wish I could have done differently, I want it to be very clear, and very tangible, which is what writing it down does for me. In this notebook, I make sure I add everything I can about my actions. I find two things particularly helpful: The first is context, which helps me better understand myself and how I might do things differently in the future. It allows me to say things like “under the circumstances, I can see I did the best I could.” The second is - is there anything here that can be set straight? For example, should I be having a difficult conversation, apologizing, forgiving? Sometimes, regret can be righted. Once I have things written down, I look them over and see if I can change the shape of this regret. I can’t change the past, but can I change how I see it? Can I be clearer on what I learned from it? Can I make very specific decisions about what I should do differently in the future, so I put it to good use? Learning from past mistakes is what makes me resilient - regret can be a tool to make the future better. Instead of shutting down, doing nothing lest it makes me feel regret again, I can say “I can do things differently” or “I am clearer on what I should say no to”. Here, I balance two things: The first is accountability (I am responsible here) and, The second is self-compassion. Am I recognizing myself as human, fallible? Or am I beating myself up for not doing everything perfectly? Am I regretting what I did (normal) or am I thinking less of myself for having done it? Regret can mean feeling stuck, feeling ashamed, feeling self-loathing. But it can also be the way towards greater self-awareness, self-compassion, growth, and full responsibility for this life that is all mine.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What can I do to worsen my decision making and performance in general life?
Answer: Prioritize pleasing others. Spend a lot of time and energy managing what others think of you so you can - Make decisions based on what others will think. Make decisions based on what others believe is best for you. Ask for many opinions, to the point you effectively drown out your inner voice. Consider every decision a life-altering decision. Overthink. Extra points if you overthink while trying to sleep. Stay up all night to make it impossible to think clearly. Multitask. Spend a ton of energy attempting to change other people. Spin up worst case scenarios. Don’t take any breaks. Rest should be something you have to earn. Consider getting things perfect your priority. If you don’t know how to do something, then don’t even try to as you will not be good at it. Don’t worry about learning to communicate. You have more important things to do than learn how to be clear. Be all things to all people. Boundaries make you difficult to like. Discard relationships. Who has time for other people anyway?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it true that hurt people hurt people? Why?
Answer: If someone hurts me it affects the way I perceive the world. My sense of safety and my sense of trust have been impacted. I become increasingly uncertain, anxious and angry. Now, my anger and my anxiety run my life. I feel I need to manage everything around me to avoid being hurt again. I do things in an attempt to keep myself safe: I am controlling, exacting, demanding, afraid, defensive. I find it hard to trust. I often perceive things as a threat, even when they are not. I become suspicious of kindness, of happiness, of peace. Blame keeps me trapped. “It’s not my fault. I hurt people because others hurt me”. Self-awareness is the first step out. “I think I am hurting others with my pain.” Taking responsibility is freedom. “I need to figure out how to work on myself so that I learn how to create healthy relationships, so I can stop hurting others and so I can learn how to stop hurting myself”.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some examples of metaphors gone wrong?
Answer: To sneak into the walled city of Troy, the Greeks built an enormous wooden horse and presented it to Trojans as a lavish gift. Once it had been taken inside the gates of the previously impenetrable city, the soldiers hidden inside defeated Troy. Saying something is “like a Trojan horse” is a metaphor for “we will present something that looks benign, and once people trust it and let it in, we will use it to destroy.” Computer viruses are a modern day equivalent: I click on a link that looks like a program I might want to use, downloading malware into my computer. I work in the tech industry and over the years I’ve heard many, many people use the term “we will be like a Trojan horse” or “this technology is like a Trojan horse” to refer to “we will use this to gain access, and once we have access, wonderful things will happen.” Over time, “Trojan Horse” has become “an unsuspecting way to gain access” and the part where once access is gained everything will be destroyed has been forgotten.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How does controlling behaviour start in a relationship? Once this behaviour exists, can it ever be a healthy relationship?
Answer: If I want to control everything, including other people, it’s because I am afraid. It’s because I am anxious. I mistakenly believe that if I can get everything and everyone around me to be how I want them to be, I will finally be safe. I walk around telling others what to do, blaming them, criticizing them, shutting them down. This means I take all the things that make me suffer - my insecurity, my uncertainty, my terror - and with it inflict suffering onto others. In many cases, controlling people are stuck. They are unhappy and wonder why their relationships are unhealthy and why patterns of aggression or even violence keep repeating themselves. In many other cases, controlling people can grow. I believe it’s possible to change controlling behavior, not in others, but in myself. Because, the only person we can ever change is ourselves. (If we attempt to change another that would make us…Yep. Controlling.) First, I become aware that I am attempting to control others. (I can’t fix something if I don’t see that I am doing it.) Then, I realize this behavior is hurting everyone, and that I need to change, for me. If I do, I will be more at peace, and my relationships will be healthier. I practice letting go of control, becoming a better communicator, and making a conscious effort to change my controlling behavior. For example, I shift from blame to taking responsibility, from being critical to learning how to complain without attacking, from seeing things in extremes to exploring a more fair middle ground. Sometimes what we suffer from the most is a case of relationship ignorance or incompetence. If what we know and what we’ve seen is to attempt to control others, we repeat this behavior. As we learn healthier ways, we adopt them and become healthier people.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I know I deserve better than him but I still can’t seem to move on. I feel like I’ll never be the person I used to be before him again. What do I do?
Answer: It’s not easy and it’s not instant and it might not be today but let me assure you: you can move on. Of course you will never be the person you used to be. Love changes us. Heartbreak changes us. Every experience changes us. We are not meant to remain the same person. This can make life better, fuller, more whole and more compassionate. This is how many hearts work: they become more robust when they break. What do you do? Believe with your whole self what you say you know. You do deserve better.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Do I need to strive to change myself to be worthy of a relationship? I'm completely confused about whether I'm worthy of a romantic partner, or whether I have toxic thoughts that love needs to be earned.
Answer: The people in my life that I love I love for free. They didn’t need to do anything for me to love them, other than be who they are: their personality, their behavior, their foibles and their flaws. There are many things these people do that I don’t like at all, that make me feel irritation or frustration or even disapproval. These things don’t make me love them any less. To review: They did not have to do anything to be loved, and do not need to be perfect to be loved. That being said, the love I feel can be nurtured. It can be nurtured through attention, through connection, through kindness. It can be nurtured through feelings of reliability and safety. I love you, and you are in my life. We come through for each other. And, the love I feel can be trashed. It can be trashed through abuse, through mistreatment, through cruelty, through lack of attention, through betrayal. We cannot count on each other. I love you, and you are not in my life. I strive to change myself. Not to become another person, but to become a better me. I want to never take for granted what has been given to me for free. I want the best, healthiest kind of love, and I want it in abundance. If you mistreat me I will mark my distance, even if my love for you is still here, intact. I don’t want people in my life who hurt me - even if the love I feel for them cannot be broken.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend said he wants to sleep with other women but doesn't want to hurt me. I said no to an open relationship, he accepted, but I feel really insecure now. What should I do?
Answer: I want to set aside the insecurity you say you feel, just for a moment - because, this is a symptom, rather than the problem you bring forth with the question you are asking. I also want to set aside any theories about how your boyfriend might or might not behave. Will he now go sleep with other women, after you said no? Maybe. Maybe not. Either way, this is speculation on things that have not taken place. I want to focus instead on the fact your boyfriend said he wants to sleep with other women, does not want to hurt you, and that you said no to an open relationship. To me, him wanting to sleep with other women does not make him wrong. It’s something he wants to do, and he is telling you he wants to do it. He is being forthcoming, expressing something he wants, which is important in relationships. He also says he does not want to hurt you, and I believe him (because, not believing someone we are in a relationship with points to bigger problems - a whole other subject that would distract from answering your question.) You said no to an open relationship, and you not wanting an open relationship does not make you wrong. You are being forthcoming, expressing a preference, which is important in a relationship. To me the issue here is that you want different things - and that wanting different things makes you incompatible. I know we hear that nothing is more powerful than love and that love conquers all but it doesn’t. Wanting different things means one of you has to make a big sacrifice. Repeatedly. Regularly. One of you will live shackled to a life different from the one you want to live. One of you will be resentful and in pain. You will live in a perpetual state of inevitable friction, and what you should do, what you both should do, is decide if that’s what you want.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the best way to cure perfectionism?
Answer: Antidotes to perfectionism: Love yourself. Love yourself because you are, not because you do. Relinquish control. Banish criticism - of others, and of yourself. Practice listening instead of defending. Invite the wide middle ground that exists between “all” and “nothing.” Stop running. Instead of being propelled by anxiety, practice being lured by something more joyful. Even if it’s hard to believe, leave room for the possibility you may already be good enough. Set aside results and enjoy the process. Explore. Practice. Experiment. Strive. Learn to bounce back from disappointment and rejection. Notice how you leave for later what you cannot do perfectly: choose “good enough” over paralysis. Try new things. Extra points if you are not good at them.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is a collective noun?
Answer: Oh boy. You are in for such a treat. The factual answer is that if you have a group of something, you need a collective noun to refer to them. The party-on-your-screen answer is that collective nouns are often arrestingly delightful. A group of falcons is called a cast. A cast of falcons. A group of crows is called a murder. A group of lions is called a pride. A group of giraffes is called a tower. Lots of paper is called a ream. Lots of arrows is called a quiver. A lot of grain is called a sheaf. A lot of poems is an anthology. A lot of bananas is a comb. A group of apes is called a shrewdness. A group of owls is called a parliament. A group of hippopotamuses is a bloat. A group of rhinos is a crash. A group of flamingos is a flamboyance. Aaaaaand, many lightning bugs are a sparkle. I mean, how absolutely enchanting are collective nouns!?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Hey everyone, I recently met someone special and I'm navigating new feelings. How can you tell if someone is genuinely interested in building a deeper relationship? What signs should I look for to know if she's really into it?
Answer: Hi! Congratulations! After much trial and error, guessing, speculating, estimating, calculating and wondering, I have learned not to look for signs. Signs are equivocal, subjective, uncertain, confusing and inconclusive. Instead, I use words: I think you are special. I am navigating new feelings and really don’t want to mess this up. I am interested in something deeper. I think we have something here. What do you think? Are you feeling the same way? Are you interested too? I am hoping we want the same things and can together work towards where we want to go. This sets a tone for honesty, clarity and even vulnerability. What better way to embark on a new relationship?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: If you go around criticizing people but you can't take any criticism when someone else criticizes you, what does that say about you?
Answer: If I go around criticizing people but can’t take criticism it means I am terribly anxious. It means I don’t think very highly of myself. It means that I am insecure, and probably have a history of being criticized, in particular when I was a kid. Because, we do what we know. It means I criticize others as a way to try to control all the things that feel unsafe to me. You never. You always. Why can’t you? Why didn’t you! You should! Criticism gives me a way to say all the things that worry me without leaving myself open to attack. People who have poor self esteem find it very difficult to be vulnerable. If I criticize others, I probably am not aware I am even doing it. It’s less about others - rather, it’s an expression of how I feel about myself. I am betraying my own insecurities, giving others a sample of what I hear all day from my inner voice. I am not condoning criticism - it destroys relationships. If I have tendency to be critical, one day I will realize how ineffective and damaging it is, and will want to become a better communicator. To complain without being critical, I avoid saying “you” and instead express what I feel and what I want. For example: Instead of: You are late again! Why are you so inconsiderate!? I try: I feel like my time is not important. If you are running late and you let me know, then I can plan accordingly. If someone is criticizing me, it helps to take a breath - to pause before responding. I might try to listen, instead of turning to defensiveness (and yes, this is really hard and takes so much practice.)
