For example, I tend to crave cookies after dinner. After dinner, I try to make it a point to go on a walk. Going on a walk, rather than watching TV, makes it a bit less likely for me to reach for a cookie, then another, then another. Remove the cookie. I have no cookies in my house. Sometimes I open all the cupboard doors cursing my decision to not have cookies and then later I am grateful that I could not find what I thought I desperately wanted. Replace the cookie. Instead of a cookie, can I have something healthier that is similar enough to a cookie to satisfy me? Live with wanting the cookie. I want a cookie. Do I have to have everything I want? Can I accept, live with the want without rushing to quench it? (I can.) Have the cookie. Not as a strategy to remove the temptation of the cookie, but because sometimes it’s the only right thing to do.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is something about yourself that would surprise the people who think they know you the best, and why would this be such a surprise?
Answer: I don’t think we ever really get to know anyone. It’s not because people are mysterious or secretive (although they can be), but because we live in our own smoke and mirrors world, tangled up in the things we assume, the things we expect and the things we project. We think others think like we think and that everyone is doing better than we are. Neither is true. Others, even people who know me well, confuse me for someone more social than I really am, more of an optimist than I actually am, happier than I am and more confident than I am. I am all of these things, but also, like you, hold contradictions and have bad days. I have regular existential crises that cripple me, and am often wracked by self-doubt which would shock the people who know me best because people see what they want to see. Many people, even close friends, say to me things like “I wish that like you I had all the answers”. It’s not that I have the answers. It’s that I am a seeker. I don’t write about what I know but about the things I need to learn. I want to have an easier go at things, and maybe to suffer less.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What do I do? I met a new friend 5 months ago. I’m scared she will end the friendship over little things. A lot of friends have left me in the past. I don’t want her to leave. I feel I need to do everything right. How do I stop feeling this way?
Answer: There are two realms in which I can exist. The first is fear. What if you leave me? I need to be perfect, get everything perfect so that you stay. I review everything I do. I review everything I say. I lie awake at night, wondering if I’ve broken something. This place is unhealthy, obsessive, full of angst and despair. If you live in fear and someone leaves you, their departure confirms what you believe to be true: you are not worthy of a good friend. The second is self love. I am decidedly not perfect. I am full of flaws and will make many mistakes. I am a good friend, despite of which, I understand I am not for everyone. I will be very clear about my needs and my preferences so that you can see me for who I am. If you decide you want to leave, I wish you well. I will be sad and I will miss you, but I will know that despite your decision I am absolutely worthy of friendship, and a hundred percent worth loving.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is seeking closure always beneficial, or are there instances where it might be better to leave things unresolved?
Answer: My definition of closure has changed over the years. It was once very specific and very concrete: we sit down, we talk, we say things like “this is over,” and only then we can move on. This left me feeling things like “I need to see this person one more time, to properly close things off.” Now, I don’t believe something can be left “unresolved” - because resolution exists inside of me. If I feel a sense that “I need closure” I realize it’s because I am going through some kind of grief. I make peace with how I feel, and give myself time. In other words, to “achieve closure” the missing ingredient is not another person, but self compassion: an ability to treat myself patiently, lovingly, respectfully. Giving myself time and space allows me to, over time, make my own declarations and my own decisions. For example: Just because I feel things for you doesn’t mean I want you in my life. I consider the way you treated me all the closure that I needed. This is not healthy. This is not what I want for myself. I don’t need you to decide for myself that this is done. I don’t need to know why another person does what they do. I don’t need another person to know if this is over or not. I don’t need “just one conversation” to “better understand.” All I need is to be gentle with myself, and decide for myself what it is that I want for me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend ruined my confidence. What should I do?
Answer: Blame is like a debilitating virus. It makes me feel judgmental, resentful, angry, ashamed, anxious and helpless and steals from me the two things that will get me through life: power and resilience. Blame robs me of anything I could possibly learn, pushes others away, and kills trust. I end up unable to see any perspective other than mine. This is how over time it causes disconnection, isolating me. Whenever I blame, I look at what I am doing and think about how I can change it. Can I love myself, so I can regard myself as flawed and identify my role in the things that happen to me? Can I acknowledge responsibility, so I can recover my agency? It’s a fact that others do awful things to us. It’s for this very reason we need to avoid blame: so we can take back the power that is rightfully ours.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: In a perfect or semi-perfect world, would being "naive" still be considered a "flaw" or would it be the norm?
Answer: The word “naive” is full of subtlety. Naive is often considered synonymous with innocence, but innocence is closer to purity, to the absence of evil, and to not wanting to cause any harm. Naive, on the other hand, is credulous, closer to showing an absence of judgement, to lacking sophistication. You might want to protect innocence, while you wish someone naive would open their eyes.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What was the coolest party you have ever been to?
Answer: On Saturday mornings my partner gets out of bed a few minutes before I do and makes coffee. We sit at the kitchen counter and I write and he draws. It’s still dark out, and as we sit there I see the sky change color, from dark to streaks of orange and pink to blue. It’s the coolest party I’ve ever been to. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What happened at a wedding that made you feel horrible for the bride?
Answer: The wedding took place in the garden. It was beautiful, and simple, and the guests were mostly family, and a few friends. At one of the tables, people started making bets over how long the couple would last. “Under a year” she said. “Under a year! Double or nothing.” She was really important to me, that person. And, she won the bet. I was the bride.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What were your thoughts and emotions while reading The Book of Life by Dushka Zapata?
Answer: Oh wow. What a coincidence. I am Dushka Zapata and have never written a book called “The Book of Life”. I am, however, working on a book that is a collection of mostly pointless life lessons - since they only prove useful once you’ve learned them for yourself. Would you write or say something if you were fairly sure no one would listen until it was too late? I think this is the fate of most “advice”. We don't listen and go and make our own mistakes and then it becomes so clear, what that person was trying so hard to tell us. This book (number 16!) will probably be published some time before the end of 2024, and I still don’t have a title for it. Hmmm. Maybe “A mostly fruitless collection of life lessons that will only prove useful once you’ve learned them for yourself.” “The book of life” is a very good title, but I hear it was taken many, many years ago. I sure hope my name is in it.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you turn a bad day into a good day?
Answer: Whenever I am having a bad day, I ask myself what I can do to reclaim it - or even reclaim a little bit of it. Can I go out for a walk? Can I get a nice cup of coffee or tea? Can I sit somewhere and read a poem? Can I call someone I love? Can I hit the pause button and take a few deep breaths? Can I sit down to a nice meal? Can we slow dance to a song we like? Can I _____ (something that brings you peace or joy)? Everyone has bad days. They are a part of life. To me it’s worthwhile to see if I can turn a bad day around. Even if I can’t, creating a moment of good within a bad day is already such a win. Over time, our memory of bad days becomes about that island of light that we created, and the bad day is just a blurry backdrop of only anecdotal consequence. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Every time my boyfriend and I argue, he brings up breaking up. What does it mean?
Answer: Are you familiar with the term “distress tolerance?” If someone has high distress tolerance they can navigate going through something difficult, like a fight. Low distress tolerance means a diminished ability to withstand being in pain or conflict. Someone with high distress tolerance might argue and feel “this is an argument. We are going to get through this, even if it’s hard.” Someone with low distress tolerance might argue and feel “this is an argument. This is the end, and I need to protect myself from the fact that this is over.” We don’t know your boyfriend and have no insight into your relationship so we cannot possibly know why he brings up breaking up. It might be because it’s what he wants. It might be a tactic to get you to stop pushing on what you are arguing about. But it might also be that to him, an argument means the end of the relationship. This means arguing is incredibly stressful to him: you are processing a disagreement, and he is processing losing you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I’m an Ethiopian teen new to distance running and everyone on the team has high expectations for me solely due to my ethnicity. How do I not let them down?
Answer: When I was a teen, letting someone down was one of my greatest fears. Oh, who am I kidding? Letting someone down is still one of my greatest fears. It keeps me up at night! What I’ve learned over thousands of sleepless nights is this: if I disappoint someone, they are not really disappointed in me, but rather in the person they thought me to be. Am I really responsible for living up to another person’s expectations of who I am and what I can do, in particular when what they expect has little or nothing to do with me? I can’t be. Living up to someone’s imagination is not just impossible, it actually sidetracks me from being true to myself. In a sense, disappointing others grants me freedom. I can stop it with the lunacy of trying to be what you want, and can start being who I actually am. This is how I claim my life as mine. What I do is the only thing I can do, and the only thing I should do: identify what I want to dedicate my time and my effort to. Get clear on my goals around that. Then, I work hard at not disappointing myself.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is it called when you tell someone about something they did that hurt you, and their response is “well you did this…”? What is that correct term that they are doing?
Answer: The behavior you describe is defensiveness, and it’s the opposite of taking responsibility. If you tell me I did something to hurt you, my instinct might be to deny it, to protect myself, to feel indignant, to shield myself from what feels like an attack. What I am doing is deflecting blame. You think I hurt you? Well, the problem is actually you! This behavior doesn’t work. It results in no one feeling heard, no one feeling understood, and as such has a tendency to make things snowball. If instead of blaming, deflecting, defending, I learn to take responsibility, it would sound like “oh no, I did do that. I can see how doing that hurt your feelings. I am sorry.” Or “You are right, I did not realize you too had a long day.” Taking responsibility is really hard, and really scary, but then the other person feels heard, and understood. Over time the relationship becomes healthier and the people in it feel like they are safe. We are aiming to understand each other, and no one is under attack.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is saying "rip" when someone passed away the most insensitive way to show condolences?
Answer: While saying “rip” is pretty bad, I can think of more insensitive things to say: “Don’t cry!” “Please don’t be sad!” “He would have wanted you to be strong.” “Just keep busy!” “He was a smoker, so this is his fault.” “Things happen for a reason.” “It was his time”. “He’s in a better place now.” “He is better off”. “Better him than me”. “This too shall pass”. “Things could be worse.” “You will feel better in no time.” “Shouldn’t you be over this by now?” “You will meet someone new in no time.”

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What word looks like it was misspell but actually it is a valid word?
Answer: Ordinance: a rule of law. Ordnance: a branch of the army that procures, stores and issues weapons, munitions and combat vehicles. Did you know this was a word? Neither did I.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why don't people mind their own business? How do you politely let them know that you want to be left alone?
Answer: I am fully responsible for this but thank you for your effort. Thank you so much for your concern, but I’ve got this. I have this covered but thank you for asking. I appreciate you, and don’t need any help for this. I would much rather handle this on my own but thank you! I actually am not looking for anyone’s support on this but thank you. To me this is a private matter but thank you. I actually want to be left alone - thank you for respecting my boundaries.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I deal with the grief from losing someone you weren’t close with? A regular customer at my job passed away, I’m not sure how to cope with my grief, as a part of me feels unworthy to grieve over what’s considerably a “stranger”.
Answer: Grief demands self compassion. Instead of “don’t be ridiculous, Dushka, you are having all these feelings for someone you didn't even know very well” I try “Dushka, what happened was awful and you deserve the space to feel. Anything you are feeling reflects who you are - a caring person who is connected to the people she interacts with”. I might also sit in a quiet place and read the beautiful poem “No man is an Island” by John Donne: No man is an island, entire of itself; Every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main. If a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less, as well as if a promontory were, as well as if a manor of thy friend’s or of thine own were. Any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Did Snoopy shoot down the Red Baron?
Answer: Snoopy is Charlie Brown’s very smart, very brave beagle. Sometimes, he is a pilot who flies a Sopwith Camel. That airplane exists in real life, and it looks like this: When Snoopy flies he flies to shoot down his mortal enemy, the Red Baron, who flies a Fokker Triplane. In real life that airplane looks like this: Snoopy never actually shoots down the Red Baron, and Charlie Brown never actually talks to the red haired girl. I love that they play endless scenarios in their head, that they live in their imagination and their angst. I think there is a little bit of Charlie Brown and of Snoopy in all of us. (Thank you to Dan Roam for teaching me about airplanes and for his contagious obsession with flight.)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Does acceptance means to give up?
Answer: A lack of acceptance means spending all my resources in attempting to alter reality. This can’t be done. It’s quixotic: acting like Don Quijote, who fought against windmills confusing them with giants. Acceptance means saying “I see things for what they are, and from this place I can organize my resources to make my battles more pragmatic, and more effective.” Acceptance is the first step towards overcoming. It’s the very opposite of giving up.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is your opinion on somebody telling you what to do if they're doing it out of love or because they care about your well being instead of just wanting control over your life?
Answer: Trying to control someone is unhealthy, but also deeply disrespectful. What I am saying is “I don’t trust you are capable”. What I am saying is “my judgement is better than yours.” What I am saying is “without me, the outcome will not be good.” The best thing we can do for the people that we love is trust that they can be responsible for their own well being. If someone said they were trying to control me “out of love” I would say “you are confusing intent with impact. If you care about my well being, the best thing you can do with your love is to take care of yourself.”

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: In your opinion, what makes someone truly beautiful?
Answer: I just finished watching the first two seasons of an Australian show called “Love me”. Everyone in the cast is so beautiful. I mention this because as the nature of the characters reveals itself, a once stunning character begins to look more or less appealing to me. I understand that what makes someone beautiful is how they look, but this holds true only briefly. It’s character that I find truly bewitching.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend cheated on me and confessed within the same 24 hours. He seems really down, sorry, and heartbroken. He told me he was drunk and blacked out, so he didn't understand what he was doing. Should I stay with him?
Answer: I have made many, many mistakes in my life and often make these mistakes more than once. Over time I have identified the shift that happens inside of me that indicates I am done with the old mistake (and ready to make new mistakes.) Do you want to know what it is, this shift? Accountability. If I make a mistake and find blame with something or someone else - it was you, it was because of him, there was traffic, why does the world conspire against me, why does this keep happening to me - I am likely to make the mistake again. If I fully own up to my mistake - this was me, and this is what I did wrong and what I should have done differently - then I am way more likely to put the mistake behind me. I cannot tell you what to do about your boyfriend cheating on you. I am so sorry to hear that you are both heartbroken. But, blaming it on alcohol, and on blacking out, saying he did not understand what he was doing? If I do not understand my own actions, there is nothing to prevent me from repeating them.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My girlfriend doesn't trust me. She's always thinking that I'm cheating. When I might just be sleeping or working. How can I make her trust me?
Answer: Ah. There is no point in writing this but you know what? I am going to do it anyway. I am going to share with you five “life lessons” you will find largely useless because they are the kind of thing you have to learn for yourself. The first: you cannot change other people. The second: you cannot “make” anyone do anything. (And get this - this holds true even if they want to do what you want to make them do.) The third: we are not responsible for another person’s emotions. This means it’s her job to be figure out how to trust, rather than your job to “make” her trust you. There is a lot you can do. You can work on being trustworthy. You can work on doing what you say you are going to do and you can work on not lying to her, not even when it feels like you are doing so “for her own good.” You can work on being true. Then, she can work on mending the part of herself that cannot trust others. She can heal, for you but mostly for herself. And, here are the two remaining life lessons, also useless, also the kind of thing that you have to learn for yourself: Four: The only thing you can ever do for your relationship is to work on yourself. And, best for last. Five: it’s true you can’t change other people, but if you are lucky love will change you. It makes you a better person. When you learn this you will want to tell everyone - but alas. No one will believe you, until they learn it for themselves.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What made you finally feel good enough?
Answer: I spent a lifetime beating myself up over what I considered to be a case of incurable relationship incompetence. From my first relationship to my last I felt I kept making every mistake and the same mistakes, over and over. I found relationships to be the most confounding, the most exhausting, the most frustrating, most heartbreaking thing ever and I would never get one right. Then, I had the strangest experience: a (long) relationship with a guy who was completely different from me. We were tragically incompatible, and living in a constant state of friction, attempting to make something work out that couldn’t, far from discouraging me, instead woke me up. One day it hit me that nothing he was doing was “bad”. We were just two distinct people. And, by extension, that also meant there was nothing I was doing that was “bad”. I was who I was, with my needs and my preferences. The relationship had no way of working, not because I was incompetent or awful but because I was me. Not because he was the villain but because he was him - and quite great, actually. Of course there is a lot of work to do to learn and grow and become better people. Better people - rather than someone we are not. I finally took in there was nothing wrong with me. This is who I am, I’m not for everyone, and that’s just fine with me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I deal with an adult child that continually brings up childhood events that did not happen the way they think they did?
Answer: Our memory is not reliable. This is, in part, because our brains revise what we remember. New experiences, new ideas, new information slightly alter or distort the way we think things happened. What this means is that it’s entirely possible for your adult child to bring up childhood events that did not happen the way they think they did. And, in equal measure, it’s entirely possible that you do not remember things the way they happened. So, instead of saying “this did not happen the way you think it did” you might try “let me tell you how I remember it” or even “I completely understand that what you are describing is how you remember it.” If you try to take away someone else’s experience by denying what to them took place - in particular if that experience has had an impact on their life and even on their identity - of course their reaction will be to defend what they believe to be true. What they are defending is not a story, but the way they see. If memory is not reliable, and two people remember things differently, each person should leave space for the validity of how another person remembers it. It’s OK - and a sign of love, and respect - to allow space for different versions of the same events. I cannot tell someone that their perception runs counter to reality. I understand that another person’s recollection of events is just as valid as mine.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why should I accept pain as a part of life?
Answer: You are not at all obligated to accept that pain is a part of life but pain is a part of life and a way to make things painful times a thousand is to be at war with the way things are. Reality is bigger than you and wider than you and is all over everything all of the time no matter how far you go to get away from it. It has no mercy and it does not relent or recede. You’ll be putting up the struggle of your life expending all the energy you’ve got and she’ll be standing around leaning on the frame of a door, making zero effort and maybe yawning not because she’s tired but because she’s bored. She will always win. Acceptance is at will but it does have a way of making things just a tiny bit easier. Up to you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend broke up with me after 3 years because his dad passed away. He said he didn’t want any priorities. We were in an amazing place in our relationship when this happened. What should I do?
Answer: Grief was so engrossing that it didn’t leave me the mind space or the heart space for anything else. It was like having my hands full of enormous boxes and having everything feel like someone was asking me to please carry something else. I can’t. I physically cannot handle anything more. So if my boyfriend needed anything from me - normal, expected things like my attention or my presence or that I pass him the salt - I couldn’t do it. This had nothing to do with how I felt towards him. Grief is quite literally a form of disability. You can’t demand anything at all from a person who is grieving. It’s like asking that they give you something they do not have (or, as we say in Spanish, asking the Elm tree to give you pears.) The only thing left to do is support the grief, not because you expect to get something out of supporting them, but because you love them. “Support” looks like different things to different people. You might check in and see how he is doing. You might attend the funeral. You might listen, or hold their hand while they say nothing. You might just have to give them space: sometimes, support has to come in the form of your absence. Because, I can’t love you right now. I can barely breathe. There is nothing you can say or do to put things back the way they were. Grief is not something to fix. Grief is what you have left of the person you once loved, and it has to move through you in its own time. I understand this can be extremely painful for the people around the person who is grieving.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are the dangers of lacking self-awareness?
Answer: Lacking self awareness is like having a faulty compass - if you can’t see where you are you can’t know where you are going. Your ability to make the right decisions is compromised. You cannot see your mistakes, so you are unable to learn from them. If you are not learning, you are not growing. You blame. Blame = lack of power. You take credit for other people’s work. The way you see yourself and the way others see you is not consistent. You wonder why you can’t seem to relate to others or why they react to you in ways you did not anticipate. You cannot see beyond your own perspective. A lack of self awareness is attributing to others things that are only related to you: why can’t I trust? Why doesn’t she make me happy? You witness circumstances around you repeating themselves, like they are chasing you. Why do I always end up in toxic situations? Why won’t anyone listen to me? Why does nobody understand me? Why are people around me so sensitive? The danger of not having self awareness is being locked in a dark room, unable to see you are the one who created it, and the one holding the keys. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are your favorite life lessons? Which ones help you lead a better life?
Answer: I want life lessons I can immediately apply. Life lessons that feel like something I can follow. Life lessons that put me in control, rather than those that assume someone else is going to do something for me. I want life lessons that feel doable, that ring true, and that accept me as flawed. Anything that demands perfection is unrealistic. My favorite life lessons are related to habits - doing a bit each day, getting back to it if I fall of the wagon - because I can do that. I can do a little each day. Or, related to a practice - practice makes me better, and accepts that “doing my best” looks different every day. A practice is such a sturdy companion to life, always there waiting for me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What would constitute a “perfect” day for you?
Answer: I suffer from what I fear is a nearly incurable affliction: my brain is always time-traveling. No matter where I am, I am thinking about what I have to do and where I have to be. Like a list of to-do’s that is always running. Like a ticker at the bottom of the screen, superimposed on whatever it is I am doing. There are two moments when I feel that all of me is right here. One is very specific: when I’m writing. When I’m writing all my inner voices pipe down. My whole system is focused on the writing. The other is more vague. It requires that I stop and take my time. Something like - from yoga class I have to run back home and clean, but what if we stop for a cup of tea between one and the other? It’s there, while I drink my tea that I can just…pause. Enjoy the tea. I will be back home soon enough. My perfect day is one pause after the other. All of me, writing. All of me, sitting on the grass. All of me walking across a museum. All of me, talking to you, basking in the privilege of your unbridled, natural enthusiasm, basking in the wonder that overcomes me when you tell me you love me. What did I ever do, to deserve this love? My perfect day is the day I feel that other than where I am there is nowhere else I need to be. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is a word for “more than happy”?
Answer: I feel ecstatic. Euphoric. Blissful. Entranced. Joyous. Exhilarated. Jubilant. Exultant. Rhapsodic. Overjoyed.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Does the English word "satisfaction" always mean something sexual?
Answer: “Satisfaction” refers to feeling content, gratified, even amused. It’s a word loaded with fulfillment, comfort, sometimes relief or vindication. I feel like I achieved what I wanted. I feel a sense of delight. I feel closure. I feel peace of mind. I feel like someone owed me and the debt has been repaid. I feel something like justice, resolution, satiety. A job well done is so satisfying. The perfect orange of that flower. The hard conversation I just had. I’ve been worried for so long and now I’m not. You hurt me and I’ve come to terms with it. I was hungry and this sandwich, wow. It’s so satisfying. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: We all know a hotdog is a sandwich, but following this logic is a taco also a sandwich?
Answer: Is a hamburger a sandwich? Yes. Is a hotdog a sandwich? Yes (but Dan Roam disagrees and refused to draw this answer accurately.) Is a taco a sandwich? Clearly, no. Is a burrito a taco? No. A burrito is a wrap. Is a quesadilla a taco? No. Does a quesadilla have to have cheese in it? No.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are hardships?
Answer: If you go through something that is dangerous, that makes you feel like you are locked in an uphill battle, struggling, like you can never feel comfortable or safe; if you are in pain, suffering, if you are being abused, oppressed, if you are exhausted, grieved, miserable, persecuted, if you feel that you cannot seem to catch a break, that is hardship.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What happened in a tent while you were camping that you will never forget?
Answer: The tent was pitched in a large garden. The floor was covered with pillows and blankets. I could see through the canvas the shadows of trees swinging in the wind. There were five of us, and we took turns telling stories. The oldest girl among us seemed reluctant. She kept skipping her turn. She went last, and blurted out that something awful had happened in that garden years before. Grown ups had pitched a tent for the kids to sleep in while they partied. No one heard or saw what happened, but in the night the kids disappeared and were never heard from again. Suddenly the tent was surrounded by many people with flashlights. Movement was sudden and confusing. The entrance to the tent was violently unzipped. I felt terror. After shrieks and screaming, the whole thing ended up being an elaborate, stupid prank and I will never forget it. I detest humor at another’s expense and won’t go near a horror movie. I stay home on Halloween.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the key for a healthy relationship?
Answer: Playing hard to get means keeping the other person on their toes through making them believe you are hard to get or like they will easily lose you. The key for a healthy relationship is exactly the opposite: In an unpredictable, painful world be a safe space for the person that you love.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some good ways to show commitment in a relationship?
Answer: Commitment means starting with me: how can I take responsibility, follow through on what I say I am going to do so my partner witnesses that I can be counted on? How can I take the best possible care of myself, so I can give the best of me? Commitment means paying attention: what are my partner’s priorities? What do they find important? What makes them feel unsafe? Commitment means taking a good look at my behavior and how it might be interpreted as hurtful or frightening to someone else and making adjustments, because love is how we grow. Commitment means doing what’s hard instead of what’s easy. Having conversations even when they are scary, truly listening, looking for the role I play when things go wrong, and telling the truth even if fibbing feels like less effort. Commitment is work. Commitment means noticing all the things the other person does well instead of all the things that bother me. Instead of being critical or nagging, saying thank you with the same insistence and urgency. Commitment means giving up on expecting perfection and understanding ourselves as flawed. Commitment is a lack of interest in fairy tales. Commitment is real.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How important it is for you to ‘build character’?
Answer: To me, “building character” looks like this: Being a participant. Setting the table. Opening the door for someone (this is not a gender thing.) Carrying the groceries from the car to the house. It’s easy to sit around letting others do things. Be the one who does them. Following through on what you say you are going to do. This to me is what makes others trust you: priceless in relationships, and perhaps the single most valuable trait at work. Practicing discipline. This is following through on what you tell yourself you are going to do. Telling the truth. Sometimes it’s easy. Sometimes it’s so hard. Do it anyway. Owning up to what you did to contribute to any unfortunate situation. This is taking responsibility. Thinking about what you could have done differently. Never in the spirit of beating yourself up. Just in the spirit of learning. Stepping up to difficult conversations. It’s possible to avoid them for years, to live under the weight of the things you are not saying. Talk. No more passive aggressive behavior. No more resentment. No ghosting. Taking care of your relationships. Your loves. Your family. Your friends. The relationship you have with yourself. Being kind. When you are feeling expansive, be kind. When you are feeling crushed, discouraged, be kind. When you are feeling exasperated, at the end of your rope, be kind. When you are feeling wronged, be kind. How important is it, to do things that build character? I don’t think there is anything more important. Things that build character make me respect myself. They strengthen my relationships. But most of all, building character is disaster preparedness: it’s the only real thing I have to fall back on when life gets impossibly hard.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Which of her books would Dushka Zapata recommend for my 18 y.o. niece? She has a mentally ill mother who neglected her and a father who manipulated the mother and her against each other. More in comment.
Answer: Hello! I recommend this one: It’s a step by step workbook about how to love yourself. It poses questions the reader has to think about and answer. My friend’s daughter, who is about the age of your niece, told me that she answers the whole thing every six months and then compares her notebooks over time. I recommend this exercise so much, to get to know yourself better. I hope she finds it supportive and useful.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it ok to purposely fade away from being friends with someone that has a crush on me? He is acting like my boyfriend/very entitled and I don't enjoy our friendship anymore because of it.
Answer: While “purposely fading away” sounds like an easy way out, it actually lacks clarity and for this reason can be extremely painful and confusing to everyone. It has a tendency to make things worse: it generates confusion, anxiety, anger. Also, having difficult conversations is a profound act of self care - the emotional equivalent of an organized house with fresh flowers on my desk. I might say “you are very important to me but lately I feel uncomfortable and trapped. I no longer enjoy our friendship and need to take time away from this relationship that is causing me stress. My hope is that you can respect my boundaries and give me the space I am asking for.” Talking about how I am feeling (I feel uncomfortable) rather than about what he is doing (you are acting entitled) is helpful in avoiding the other person interpret what I am saying as a personal attack. Of course, none of this would not apply if my friend was showing signs of becoming abusive, or if I felt in any way unsafe. But, overall, defaulting to being as clear as possible and taking full ownership of the decisions that I make lays out a path for a better life, for everyone around me, and for me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it normal if someone you’re friends with all of a sudden stops hanging out with you because they think you have gotten boring? Or they’re not interested anymore? And also were they even a real friend to begin with?
Answer: Life is change. Feeling close to someone and then not feeling close is a natural part of life. It’s actually extremely rare for any relationship to last forever. (Of course, the fact that it’s natural doesn’t mean it doesn’t hurt.) The first times this happens, no one has the life skills to know how to manage it, so it turns into something extremely painful that we tend to feel somehow defines us. In other words, if someone doesn’t want to hang out with me, it does not make me any less worthy of friendship. It does not mean I am not good enough. It does not mean they were never a real friend or that I was never important to them. It just means things change. The way to navigate this is to remain very close to ourselves and our own trajectory. To understand, even as we change, who we are and what we want. To be able to say “I think this friendship has run its course, and that is a part of life.” And to communicate clearly, as a part of handling things with grace. “I love you so much. You are such good friend. I think we are hanging out less because we are changing. I don’t think we can resist what is happening but I do want to tell you that I love you and that I will be here for you even as we don’t see each other as much as we used to. This is not a fight or a falling out - it’s just what life does.” And then, instead of dreading a call from a friend, instead of feeling like hanging out doesn’t feel right anymore and forcing things, instead of feeling resentful, we surrender to the terribly bittersweet evolution of our friendships - without questioning what we once had, and without it having to mean we are now obligated to become enemies. It’s ok to part ways and love each other, and know that what we had mattered.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What do I do if my boyfriend told me that he is alone and no one is standing by his side? What am I to him?
Answer: If my boyfriend told me “I am alone and no one is standing by me” I think the first flare of a reaction from me would be “Me. I am standing by you.” I think him feeling alone would hurt me. I have vowed to be compassionate towards myself and any reactions I might have, so to this I would tell me: “of course it hurts, Dushka. That’s normal. But right now, your boyfriend is saying he feels no one is standing by him. He is in pain. So, let’s not make his pain about us.” When someone else is expressing pain, I have to practice setting myself aside to be there for them. Listening is about being fully there for the other person. It’s about being respectful about whatever they might be feeling, without judgement. I don’t have to agree, or disagree, or say it’s good or bad. I don’t have to refute it or argue with it. I don’t need to fix it. But more than anything else - this is about him. I can’t make it about me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What should I do if my boyfriend asks me to do something I don't want to do, and then tells me we can't talk or see each other until I do it?
Answer: If my boyfriend asks me to do something I don’t want to do and then tells me we cannot talk or see each other until I do it, I realize I have two choices: To compromise my relationship with him to stand up for myself To compromise my relationship with me to do what he asks me to do. To me, this is an easy decision. I stand up for myself. I look in the mirror and say “Dushka, if you don’t want to do something, I’ve got your back.” I don’t have to say anything at all to my boyfriend, since he’s taken care of it all by saying we can’t talk or see each other until I do something I am never going to do.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I love my boyfriend, so why am I wishing he would do something wrong so I can leave?
Answer: You are asking the right question but are asking the wrong people. There is absolutely no way we could know the answer. It could be because it feels like you love him, but you actually don’t. It could be because you love him, and love is scary and you want control over the unfolding of your story. Because, the loss of someone is easier to handle than the fear of losing someone. It could be because you love him but don’t want to be with him (which seems implausible but is instead entirely possible.) It could be because you are used to situations that are conflicting and emotional and you need to create situations that are conflicting and emotional to feel like you are in a familiar environment, because it feels safer than loving. Only one person has the correct, definitive answer, and that is you. Finding this answer is how you get to know yourself, how you get to identify and understand your patterns, and how you can alter the things you tend to do, for a happier, more peaceful life.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some examples of an emotionally immature person?
Answer: Here are four examples (and I think all four examples live in all of us at any given time.) The person who is unable to take responsibility. Everything is always someone else’s fault. “Nobody” understands them. “Everyone” wrongs them. They never ask “what role did I play in the situation I find myself in?” The person who is always at the center of the story. Everything is personal. It’s all about them. They tend to fish for compliments and reassurance. “I’m so sorry that I can’t get anything right.” The person who cannot make the connection between their action and the consequences. For example, they have an extravagant lifestyle and then cannot make financial ends meet, but cannot seem to adjust their extravagant lifestyle. Instead, they borrow money from everyone. The person who knows just what to say to hurt your feelings. Your reaction - startled, perplexed, wounded - is how they feel they have connected, like a boxer landing the punch. Their reaction is always invalidating: you can’t take a joke. You know I didn’t mean that. Why are you so dramatic? Why do you make such a big deal out of everything? The best thing to do? Remain vigilant to when one of these examples is me. Am I taking responsibility? Am I making things about me? Am I seeing the consequences of the decisions that I make? Am I being hurtful or invalidating? How to best handle when other people are being emotionally immature? Don’t get roped in. Don't try to help or fix or save them (resist being the enabler.) Trust that they will figure things out. Trusting someone to figure it out is not abandonment. It’s a mark of respect. It’s believing they are capable: Knowing they can and will grow up. If we can do it, so can they. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How would you describe the difference between a blank stare and vacant eyes?
Answer: If you say something and I don’t know what to do or what to say, I may give you a blank stare. It’s what my eyes look like if you’ve left me speechless or nonplussed. If I have been staring at my phone or at the TV for hours or maybe if I am depressed - any event that has drained my brain of its zip - you might get a vacant stare: empty, devoid of thought or emotion.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How does establishing healthy boundaries in relationships and learning to say no contribute to better mental health and self-esteem?
Answer: Have you ever felt exhausted, overextended, resentful, like everyone is taking advantage of you, asking you to do for them things you learn they are not willing to do for you? Have you felt that fury, that isolation, that sense of unfairness, that outrage? Have you ever felt completely overwhelmed? With boundaries, that nightmare is over.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How does engaging in acts of self-care, such as taking time for hobbies or pampering oneself, contribute to overall mental wellness?
Answer: Engaging in acts of self-care is how I uphold my mental health. But, I don’t think hobbies and “pampering myself” are how I would define self-care. To me, self care is what I do to protect myself. For example, learning how to say no and setting boundaries. Having difficult conversations to deepen and improve my relationships. Giving up on “keeping the peace” and instead learning how to communicate so I can represent myself better. Taking time to rest and learning to do so without guilt that I am not being productive enough. To be there for myself with compassion when I am anxious, overthinking or unable to sleep. Self care is about keeping an eye on my expectations to better understand my recurring disappointment. Self care is about learning how to listen. Of course, taking time for hobbies and pampering myself plays a role - a massage is, after all, very nice - but to me mental wellness runs deeper and is grittier and more uncomfortable. If you think exfoliating is good, wait until you look in the mirror and say - I love you, and you are the one responsible for our issues. Let’s get to work on understanding the role we play in what happens to us. The assumption that pampering myself is conducive to mental health is like placing a bandage very close but not on top of the blister that keeps me from enjoying my walk through life. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it okay to act okay when you are not okay?
Answer: Saying I am OK when I am not, or acting OK when I am not, is the same as creating a complex labyrinth from other people to my well being. How are they supposed to find me? How are they supposed to know? How are they supposed to understand me? How are they supposed to support me? Saying “I am not OK” is like an arrow. Saying “I am not OK, here is what is happening to me and here is how you can help” sets me on a more fortunate path. Please. Let’s assist rather than hinder the people who care about us. Let’s not give others an impossible assignment. (I drew this one)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can I help my mother with diabetes?
Answer: The same golden rule that applies to every relationship and every love and every dynamic with every person we have ever cared about applies to parents: we cannot change, help or save anyone but ourselves. We can’t get others to do what we think is best for them. We can’t get them to pick up habits that we think will help them. We can’t, no matter how much we talk, get them to see what they don’t see. We can’t witness them do something that we think is wrong or unhealthy or might get them sicker and feel overwhelmed with sadness and frustration and talk to them and expect this will somehow result in a different behavior. It will not. What it will do is leave us depleted, grieving, exasperated and resentful. It will leave us wondering how we can put so much energy, care and passion into something that. Will. Not. Budge. Here is what we can do for others - including our parents. We can accept. We can realize it’s not our job to give them long lectures about how they should live their life. It’s not our job to give up our own structure and peace of mind. Not our job to give them all our time and all our grit. It our job to look at them closely and learn and vow not to repeat what they are doing, since there is quite a bit of them inside of us. We can turn our energy and focus back on ourselves and straighten out our own habits, our own life, our own health. And, they can do the same for themselves. Living with diabetes requires change, deep change, and only she can do this. We can support this change. Support their efforts, rather than take it on as if it was ours. We can love them, love them with all our hearts, and all our respect. I respect you enough to trust you are capable of rising to the occasion and taking care of yourself. I can’t do it for you. Even if I completely abandoned my own life to dedicate it all to you, it still would not be enough if you are not actively taking care of yourself.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What am I supposed to do now in life?
Answer: Oh no. I urge and implore you never to ask what you are supposed to do. If I ask what I’m supposed to do, I end up doing what I believe is expected of me instead of doing what is right. This is how so many people who do what they believe they are supposed to do end up sitting in a living room they seldom use on a couch they rarely sit on and wonder how on earth this is their life. Is this all there is? How do I escape this place I ended up in? Instead, I want to ask - how can I be more self-aware, to really know what it is that I want? What am I willing to dedicate myself to in a way that has a measure of meaning, and of joy? What can I do so life doesn’t feel like a grind, like a loop, like low-grade despair? If I confuse what I am supposed to do with something I want, do I really understand what it entails? Do I fully grasp what I am getting myself into? Ask instead - who am I? What do I want? What do I feel I am meant to do? And then say - I don’t care what I am supposed to do. I alone bear the burden of the consequences of my decisions and as such I will instead move towards what is right for me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is your "golden rule" when it comes to relationships?
Answer: Communicate. Every time I become discouraged and decide the conversation “is not worth it,” Every time I feel like he should “just know” instead of exploring and then clearly expressing what I want, Every time I make assumptions instead of asking questions, Every time I choose to say nothing instead of working on how to put into words what I am thinking or feeling I am disinvesting in the relationship. Every time I set aside “winning the argument” or forcing my point of view and become truly hungry to understand the other person’s perspective, the relationship gets stronger.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do people say that "relationships take work"?
Answer: Because dreaming of a fairy tale wedding is easy, and becoming a stronger couple when things get hard takes work. Because pretending everything is “fine” is easy and putting love, energy and time into understanding each other takes work. Because, feeling like “he should just know” is easy, and learning how to ask for what I want takes work. Because white lies are easy and telling the truth takes work. Because being aloof and dismissive is easy and making sure you are a safe person even when you are angry takes work. Because giving up when things get rocky is easy and learning how to communicate is work. Because staying angry is easy and forgiving takes work. Because blame is easy and taking responsibility is work. Because saying yes to everything and then feeling resentful is easy and good boundaries take work. Because thinking only of what works for me is easy and being a team is work. Because looking for someone to “make me happy” and “complete me” is easy and working on myself takes work. Constant work. The best work.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is there someone out there that will treat me right?
Answer: Wondering if there is someone out there who will treat me right is so painful, like hope has, over time, seeped out of me. I feel discouraged. I feel exhausted. Do you know what I need? I need to step away from it all and get a few good nights of sleep. Then, I need to get a notebook and write down the things that keep happening to me. Do I end up in relationships with someone abusive? Or with someone who tries to control me? Or, in one sided relationships, where I seem to care and the other person doesn’t? Am I chasing people who are not interested, convinced that if only I could make them see, I would find happiness? I cannot break a pattern I am not aware of. As my patterns emerge I need to learn new things, so I explore all the wisdom that is available online, and in books. How can I communicate better? How can I create better relationships? How can I double down on what is good for me and walk away from what is bad for me? I take a look at my habits, and the things that I practice, because they hold the tight buds of what my life will become. Am I resting well? Eating well? Is exercise a part of my daily life? What would I like to accomplish in the future, and am I taking small steps to get there? What about my space? Do I have a place that feels safe, where I can gather myself at the end of a long day? Can I work on keeping it neat and clean, surround myself with things that are meaningful to me, like photos of characters I love, books I’d like to read, a few beautiful plants, a colorful set of bowls? What about finding something I want to create? Do I want to paint, bake, make a collage, take some photos? Do I have pens and coloring books? One day, I get up early in the morning and go on a nice long walk. I go to a pet shelter to volunteer and spend some time petting and brushing a pup. Later, I take myself on a date: I check out a frozen yogurt place I’ve been meaning to try, and catch a movie. I love witnessing the reactions of people around me. I like the immersive nature of a gigantic screen. And that’s when it hits me. Of course there is someone out there who will treat me right. I have me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Are the terms "feelings" and "expressions" close in terms? How so and how not?
Answer: What is your emotional state? Overwhelmed, sad, joyful, hopeful, anxious? These are feelings. What are you communicating, indicating, with your body language, your speech, your writing, your sketches, your interpretative dance? These are expressions. The way I make my emotional state evident to others is through how I express them, but it’s also possible for what I express to not represent my feelings at all. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend said he needs space because he no longer loves me and he needs to get back his feelings. He stopped texting/calling and he said he is not breaking up with me. Should I break up with him?
Answer: I don’t know what you should do. This is because the two of you have a history and context that I cannot possibly know about. What I can tell you is that if my boyfriend said he needed space because he no longer loved me, I would definitely consider that a breakup. I love him very much, and what I deserve is for someone to feel about me the way I feel about them. Waiting around for him to maybe call, to maybe text, wondering if he will come back today, or tomorrow, or never, would be excruciating, and I would not put anyone through that kind of torture. If I wouldn’t put someone else through something like that, why would I do it to me? You go, my love. Go find the time and space you need. I hope you find what you are looking for.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can you deal with someone who can only see one side of an argument?
Answer: Healthy conflict requires the ability to see more than one perspective: I believe I have a point, I can see you do too, and I grasp that they are equally important. Emotional immaturity means I can only see my side of the argument. I cannot acknowledge the possibility of more than one vantage point. If I am emotionally mature, other perspectives open my world. They lead to understanding, and as a result, stronger relationships. If I am emotionally immature, other perspectives threaten me. They make me feel attacked, so I become extremely defensive. I am not defending my argument, but my sense of self. This means I resort to blame, look to dominate conversations, talk to many other people in search of confirmation that my views are in fact correct. It’s important to remember we cannot change other people. We cannot demand they give us something they do not have. (I mean, we can, but we won’t get very far.) To navigate interactions with people who refuse the existence of other perspectives, I need very strong boundaries. I need to check my expectations: remind myself not to argue with someone who is unable to listen or understand. And, the most important thing: remain steady, so I don’t get sucked into belligerent, aggressive dynamics that ultimately gets me nowhere and leaves me frustrated, exhausted and alone.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can I make him realise my worth and get him to love me again?
Answer: The conviction that I could “get” someone to love me, that I could somehow “get” someone to realize I was worth their attention and their love, is the single biggest way I have wasted my energy and my time. It’s the way I’ve hurt me the most. “Getting” someone to feel a certain way has distracted me from seeing who they are. Who they are is not interested. This is not some unattainable, irresistible creature. It’s just someone who is not interested in me. And me expending effort to get them to change feels like such a rush that I confuse it with being in love. So here is my hard-earned lesson: love is not ever something to chase. It requires no persuasion, no convincing, no winning over. Instead, I take all that effort and spend it learning how to communicate. On learning how to represent myself for who I am. Here is the equation that I believed: A lack of interest in me = if only I could make you see. Here is the equation that evaded me so many years: A lack of interest in me = a person who is not good for me. We all deserve someone who is as interested in us as we are in them. Then, we can both put effort into communicating better and creating a better relationship. Now that is time well spent.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it wrong to not talk to your abusive mother anymore?
Answer: There is one person in the world who knows the answer to this question, and that’s you. I urge you to disregard what anyone else has to say. It’s easy for people who are not in your situation to tell you things that make sense from their vantage point and not from yours. “Family is the most important thing.” “I could never stop talking to a parent.” “You have to work this out.” Of course these things are true - for them. Except, some parents are not loving. Or supportive. Or healthy. Sometimes, a person has to stop talking to a family member to find sanity. No relationship is supposed to hurt you. It doesn’t matter who that relationship is with. It doesn’t matter if someone who is in a safe, loving relationship with a supportive parent feels that what you’re doing is wrong. Here’s what matters: that you do what you need to do to keep yourself safe and well, to find peace. And yes. This decision can irreparably break your heart.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can I get rid of overthinking?
Answer: Overthinking if a form of paralysis that feels like action. “It’s not that I’m not doing anything - it’s that I’m thinking about what to do.” It’s what my brain does when she is scared and wants me to stay safe. It’s her way to keep me comfortable: I am going to get you stuck in the endless loops of your own thoughts so that you don’t have to decide, don’t have to feel discomfort, don’t have to feel inadequate. This is how we will avoid all risk. The way to get rid of overthinking is to treat it like white noise. My thoughts will always be there, unremovable, humming in the background, analyzing every angle, presenting me with all the worst case scenarios. I can decide that my thoughts are valuable, but not necessarily true. I can tell my brain things like “that can definitely happen, but also what if it doesn’t?” Tell me. What if things work out? If my overthinking ran my life I would never do anything. I would never even leave my house. Thank you for paralyzing me with all your thought-ammunition but I’m going to go ahead and do what I think is best for me. I will go ahead and live.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is one surefire way to improve your game at life?
Answer: We wish someone would just tell us what to do. We believe others have the answers, so we look to them in our time of need. Instead of asking “how does this make me feel?” we wonder how we can find someone to give us advice, shutting out our own inner voice. To know what to do next, to find the best guidance, to find the answers - look within. Every time we look to ourselves, we fine-tune our ability to find the answers that exist inside of us. We are the only experts in the path of our own life.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Should a man get in touch with his feminine side to be more understanding?
Answer: I cannot possibly believe “understanding” is a feminine trait. Or, tenderness. Or, vulnerability. Or sensitivity. Or being nurturing, or full of grace. I don’t buy that “intuition” is somehow only for women. Similarly, I cannot possibly believe that aggression is masculine. Or, assertiveness. Or, strength. Or dominance. I think we would all be healthier, more secure and less repressed if we stopped attributing things to a specific gender and allowed each individual to be everything they are, in all their radiance and splendor.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: He says he loves me but is depressed and does not want to talk to me in any way, does he love me? Or am I being strung along? I love him more than anything but this hurts
Answer: One of the most dangerous things my brain does is make excuses for someone’s behavior. Here is what I mean: Someone will act in a way that is not considerate or not respectful or that is dismissive or even cruel and my brain will say “well, he must be going through a very hard time.” Or, “he was really hurt in a previous relationship” or “he is depressed and struggles with being vulnerable.” So, I justify. I spend a lot of energy making excuses until I create for myself a small dark cell where being treated in this way becomes somehow OK. I become stuck in a heartbreaking dynamic where I am always wondering why there is no light here and why love hurts so much. The fact is this: we all go through extremely difficult things and it’s our responsibility to show an ability to connect to others. It’s also my responsibility to stop it with the excuses and accept when another person cannot give me what I want. An absence of acceptance means I keep breaking my own heart. To more specifically answer your question, we don’t know this man so cannot possibly know if he loves you or is stringing you along. More to the point, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter because “he does not want to talk to you in any way”. If someone tells me “he does not want to talk to me in any way” then I owe it to myself to stop demanding that someone give me what they do not have.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Don't be kind to everyone. Not everyone deserves kindness, you cannot afford to be kind with those who aren't kind to you. Do you have self-dignity and respect?
Answer: What if. What if kindness is not related to what others do or don’t deserve, but to the fact that the way I treat others has an impact on my regard for myself? In other words, what if kindness builds self-confidence? What if kindness is a mark of self respect? What if being unkind robs me of how good it feels to be kind? What if kindness is the great connector, and protects me from feeling isolated? What if being kind is about dignity and respect, rather than something that compromises dignity and respect? What if being unkind and rude diminishes me, and being kind, even to those who are not kind to me, fortifies my character, strength training for my personality? What if someone who is unkind is going through something awful and has a completely empty tank, easily replenished by a little kindness? What if being kind to everyone was a virtuous circle in a world burdened by too many vicious circles? Being unkind leaves me feeling really meh. Honestly - I can’t afford it.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is jealousy proof that someone loves you or that they want to control you?
Answer: Jealousy is a mark of insecurity and inadequacy. It means I am afraid someone can take away something I consider to be mine. Jealousy is related to my inner state and the regard I hold myself in - not related at all to how I feel about someone else. It’s possible for me to feel a pang of jealousy in relation to someone I don’t care about; and feel no jealousy in relation to someone I love. Confusing jealousy with love is unhealthy. It means I feel loved by someone who is attempting to control me to control their own emotions. It means I confuse someone wanting to possess me with someone wanting what’s best for me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some good questions I should ask myself every day?
Answer: I have a tendency towards anxiety and a brain that spins worst-case scenarios, even when I don’t ask her to. I have a list of questions I ask myself that loosen the grip of “what’s the worst that can happen?” and help change my perspective without ever being forced optimism. Here they are: What if everything works out? (I love this question so much it’s the screensaver on my phone.) What if all the best things have not yet taken place? What if things turn out better than you thought they would? What if you are just right? What if this gigantic problem that seems unsolvable solves itself? What if this thing that you’ve lost is making room for something better for you? What if instead of trying harder to control what’s out of your hands, you surrender?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Will I ever love anyone like I loved her?
Answer: My experience is that every love is different. It’s like each one is made with a unique combination of ingredients - commitment, danger, chemistry, friendship, trust, insanity, romance, playfulness, lust, affection, intimacy, passion, a bond, to name a few - and each has these things in varying measures. From what I have felt, I do not think you will ever love anyone like you loved her. You loved her the way you did because of who you were at that time, and who she was; because of what you were both going through, and what you created together. Because of the way she’d hold her bright red cup with both hands without drinking from it. These things cannot be replicated in exactly this way. This love that you had for her was molded by who she was and what you had to give. You may love someone else more, though. Or with more lust. You may love madly. You may love them well in a way that is new and that cannot compare to anyone before or after. I don't believe the first love is the great love or that we love just one person. Throughout our life we get to love many people in many ways. And, if we pay attention, if we are willing to practice and apply ourselves, we don’t just love again but love better, thanks in great part to what we’ve learned from loving the people we’ve loved.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some things that are out of your control?
Answer: What I cannot control: The passage of time, the longevity of anything that matters to me, economic fluctuations, meteorological conditions, natural and unnatural disasters, getting sick and getting old. What others do and how they choose to behave, what others consider important, the boundaries others set, their feelings, what they decide to change or not change; what others think, what others think of me. A lot of what happens to me, the result of my own efforts, the consequence of my actions and my decisions: because, life happens, I can fail despite my best work, and I can make many good decisions and still not obtain the outcome I wanted. More things I don’t really control but can nurture and practice: What I say, what I do with my time, how I experience my emotions, the things I feed and protect, how I care for myself, where I put my attention and my energy, how I handle myself when things don’t go my way, the boundaries I decide to set, the boundaries I hold, how I choose to interpret things, and my moment by moment struggle to stay right here, right now instead of thinking of what I have to do and where I need to be.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you set boundaries and have difficult conversations without ruining relationships/friendships?
Answer: No matter how I do it, no matter the skill and the tact, setting boundaries and having difficult conversations will absolutely ruin some of my relationships. It will ruin my relationships with people who want me to be the way they want, instead of the way I am. Who want me to do things for them at the cost of what I need to do for me. People will call me selfish, for turning my attention and my resources to what is best for me, instead of what is best for them. Setting boundaries and having difficult conversations will strengthen my relationships with everyone who respects that I - like every other human - have limits. The people willing to navigate difficult conversations with me are the people I want in my life. Those who say “my relationship with you is worth me being uncomfortable as we work through this.” I know this is hard to hear, but boundaries and difficult conversations are filters. They ruin relationships that were never healthy; and strengthen relationships with people who are willing to love me, respect me, and accept me for who I am. Boundaries and difficult conversations are not selfish. They are what I need to do to give the best of myself to others. Without them, I am perpetually overextended and resentful. Without them, I give everything and wonder why everyone around me takes advantage of me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it normal to say hurtful things in a relationship when we're fighting?
Answer: Saying hurtful things when you are fighting is common, but it’s not good. Hurting the person you are in a relationship with causes cracks in the relationship. It weakens it, shakes its foundation. If someone hurts me I end up unable to trust them, unable to feel safe around them, and a relationship cannot survive this (or, can’t survive this and remain a healthy relationship.) Fighting cannot and should not be avoided. A healthy relationship is not about not fighting, but about fighting well. Fighting well means: I stand up for myself and feel safe in doing so, rather than standing up for myself and feeling I am jeopardizing the relationship. I show up willing to take responsibility. Fights take two. I am at least partially responsible. I am very mindful and gentle about how I start a fight, because how I start will determine how it develops (if I attack you, you will feel defensive. If I start gently, you will be more open to listening.) So, I state my case without blame. It helps to start with how I feel. “I feel like my time is not important” is different from “you are so thoughtless when you are late.” I attempt to be as considerate, as loving and as respectful as I can. If I am too angry to do this, I say “I want this conversation to go well and need some time to sort myself out. Let’s talk tomorrow.” Other things that help me a lot are: do not hold things in. Do not convince yourself “it’s not worth the conversation”. Do not fight when angry. Always be willing to listen. Do not argue to win. Never make another person feel unsafe. (The fact that I am leaving this for tomorrow is because I want to do it right. I love you so much.) And, if I ever say something hurtful, I apologize and mean it.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What if you feel like you can't get over being bullied?
Answer: Humans go through terrible, awful things. Going through something frightening or painful and being told “you will get over this” can feel invalidating, like all of the things you are feeling are somehow just fluff, shake-off-able. (Don’t you see? Don’t you see how this thing that happened to me has stolen something from me, has made me another person that I do not think I can recover?) I don’t want to do that. I don’t want to make less of what you now feel. Instead, I want to reply with a fact: humans consistently underestimate their own resilience. After surviving horrible things, we can grow. We are caterpillars, capable of metamorphosis. We feel stuck and devastated and then things click and we find a sense of meaning in what has happened to us. This does not mean “things happen for a reason”. It means we work hard to make sense of what we’ve been through. It does not mean we are not extremely hurt: it means we are strong despite of what has happened to us. We understand the suffering of others better. We develop empathy. We decide what we want to stand for. We are more clear on who we are. It’s not that we “get over it”. It’s that we are forged by what we have been through. Recommended reading: Man’s Search for Meaning, by Viktor Frankl

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: When I don’t feel respected in a relationship (with a partner or friends), how do I know if it is just my ego or the person is actually being disrespectful?
Answer: To me, the fact that you are even asking this question is a mark of self-awareness. Feeling hurt, slighted or treated poorly triggers an emotional response, and it takes real presence of mind to say “wait a minute. What if this is me?” Put in other words, you are already doing the most difficult part, which is to notice, then question yourself and your perception. To me, the next step is self-compassion, and standing up for myself. The ability to say “if you feel hurt, Dushka, that is valid. We will get to the bottom of this together.” (Rather than saying, Dushka you are being too sensitive. Suck it up.) Then, I would talk to my friend or partner. “I feel disrespected. I want to talk through it, because I am open to the fact that it might be my ego.” A good friend who is also self-aware might say something like “I can totally see how what I said could come across poorly. I am really sorry.” This kind of conversation is what deepens relationships and makes them stronger. The ability to talk about difficult things. Finally, I would observe if this feeling comes up frequently. Do I want to say something like “everyone always disrespects me?” If a sensation starts with “everyone” or “always” that points to a pattern: an indication that there is something I need to calibrate within me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do people feel old in their thirties when they probably have most of their life still ahead of them?
Answer: I don’t think I ever feel old because of my age, or how much time I may have ahead of me. I feel old because: That thing that took place happened so much longer ago than I remember. (The terrorist attack on the WTC and The Pentagon was 22 years ago.) That place I expected I would be by now is not where I am. I allude to something incredibly common and no one knows what it is because, alas. They happen to be decades younger than I am. (Dushka, what do you mean by “mixed tape”?) I used to be excited to do something that now sounds like the last thing I want to be doing. (No thank you I don’t want to go to the concert and stay up all night.) I used to be able to do something that now I cannot do. (No thank you, I can’t go to the concert and stay up all night.) I find myself saying things like “oh my god look how much you’ve grown!” and “just wait until you…” There is a mismatch between how old I feel and how old I actually am. (Why do I have to scroll so much before I can find the year I was born if I feel like I’m 20?) I catch a glimpse of my reflection and don’t recognize her.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Have you ever met your school bully as an adult?
Answer: When I was a kid, maybe around 11 years old, there was a girl in my class who terrified me. She was observant, insightful and incredibly mean. She had a way of mocking me that made me feel vulnerable and exposed. Years later, when I was maybe 16, I was talking with my group of friends about people who made us feel bad, or small, or scared when we were younger. We all mentioned her by name - this girl and her ability to know just what to say to decimate, humiliate or ridicule us. Decades later, I was shocked to see her name in my inbox. Just seeing her name felt stressful to me, even after so many years. I opened the email full of trepidation and a tiny bit of curiosity. Her message to me was a thank you note, something like “I am so grateful for the beautiful, useful things you write on your Instagram page. My daughter is having a really hard time at school, as she is the frequent target of bullies, and your writing really bolsters her spirit. We often talk about your daily posts over dinner.” The fact that how she once made me feel in some way inspired the writing that has helped her kid survive high school is very powerful to me. I think it’s what pain is for.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why would a guy act like he has a crush on you one day, almost ignore you the next, and flip back and forth between those all the time?
Answer: To me, attempting to figure out why people do what they do is futile. It’s a way to expend so much energy, to ultimately accomplish nothing. Whenever I find myself wondering why this person or that person did this or that, I think about what it would sound like if I turned the question back to me. Why, Dushka? Why do you spend even a moment of your time thinking about someone who makes you feel perplexed, uncertain, ignored, unpredictable and unsafe?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why does a guy like you but won't ask you out?
Answer: Because, asking someone out is scary. Because, he wants to avoid rejection. Because, he doesn’t want to get hurt. Because, he just went through a bad breakup and he’s had enough. Because, he is really shy. Because, he does not have a good read on how you feel about him. Because, you are good friends and he doesn’t want to jeopardize that. Because, he is waiting. For a sign. For the optimal moment. For the light to hit just right. Because, he likes you but also likes other people and he can’t decide who to ask out.
