Because, he likes you but is not interested in dating you. Because, he likes you but is not interested in a relationship. Because he likes you but is not interested in a relationship with you. Because, he likes you but is in a relationship with someone else. Because he likes you but is in love with someone else. Because he is wondering why on earth you like him and are not asking him out.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you distinguish being selfish from setting boundaries or saying no?
Answer: Being selfish benefits no one. Setting boundaries benefits everyone.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the best misunderstanding story worth sharing?
Answer: I once met a guy through work. Over time, we became quite close. One early evening, we were on a video conference and he said something like “I think we’ve become such good friends.” I try to be as clear as possible when I communicate, even when it scares me, so I gathered all my courage and blurted “I don’t think we are friends.” His (completely understandable) interpretation was “we are not as close as you think we are.” What I meant was “I think this is the beginning of a love story.” Without intending to, I scared the crap out of him twice. Once when he didn’t understand me, and then again when he did.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why didn't he care when I broke up with him?
Answer: I see three possible reasons. He did care, and did not want to show it. He did not love you, and so when you broke up with him, he felt relieved. The relationship had been bad for a while, so he processed the end of it before it was actually made official.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you prepare for life?
Answer: If something out there scares me, intimidates me or discourages me, and I move away from it, it shrinks me. It circumscribes me. If something out there scares me, intimidates me or discourages me and I go through the effort of figuring it out, it informs me. It expands me. The best way to prepare for life is to try. Trying is learning, and the more I learn the more able I become.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the difference between a fact and a principle?
Answer: A fact is reality. It exists. It happened. It’s truth. It’s objective. An opinion is a personal view. It’s subjective. A principle is a primary rule. It’s essential, fundamental, and often serves as a guide.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do we, as humans, stop the urge to be in control? How can we accept that nothing is in our control and still live bravely and happily?
Answer: We try to control things around us when we feel unsafe. In an attempt to shield myself from an unbearable uncertainty, I exert control over the things I feel I can. Maybe if my house is in order I can keep chaos at bay. Trying to control everything comes from a place of stress and fear. It’s exhausting, because we don’t really have control over anything. Control is contrary to reality, and attempting to contradict reality will make me sick. What helps me feel at peace is enjoying the moment I am in - this is the opposite of imagining what could possibly happen in the future. It helps me to notice when I am trying to get everything perfect. Be careful. There is no way to do that. Let it be good enough. And mostly, looking at my own past and reminding myself of all the things I have overcome. I may not be able to control anything, but I have shown me that I am capable. It’s this trust in myself and my own ability that soothes my urge to control all the things I cannot possibly have any power over.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My boyfriend said that his love was plastic. Did he love me or not?
Answer: If someone says their love is plastic, I might interpret his love as artificial, as fake. I might take it to mean it has no depth or warmth. I might understand his love as chemical, toxic, pollution instead of breath. Plastic love is rigid love, love that pretends to be things it is not. Or, plastic is everywhere. It’s strong, infinitely pliable, can be molded into any form. It’s plastic, imagination. There is no limit to what it can create. It’s adaptable, resilient. It withstands time and any weather. Maybe plastic love is forever love. We don’t know, from what people say, if they love us or not. Words. They are plastic.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why did my ex-boyfriend instantly start talking to other girls as soon as we broke up even though he said he loved me more than anything in the world? Isn’t he feeling the pain like I am?
Answer: How I react after a breakup is not related to how I felt during the relationship. It’s not related to the amount of pain I am in. It’s related to my emotional maturity - to the way I process my own emotions. Many people cannot date or even socialize, and others socialize or date in an attempt to feel better. To quote The Eagles, “some dance to remember, some dance to forget.” To better understand how to recover from a breakup, I need to remember just one thing. Here it is: How I process what I am feeling - lost, hopeless, anxious, empty, betrayed - shows me who I am. Let me say it differently: the way I witness myself handling my emotions will result in either self-love or self-loathing. My own behavior will build or shatter my confidence. So, how can I do better when it comes to a breakup? I can work on my communication skills. By this I mean I can fight to understand rather than to hurt, I can relinquish having to be right, I can keep in mind two very different perspectives can both be correct and valid. I can make room for all my feelings, learn to make them my companions, instead of finding distractions or using other human beings as an ineffective escape to my pain. I can show compassion, towards myself and the person I am breaking up with. Compassion towards myself means minding my inner dialogue (from “I am unlovable” to “this relationship not working is not related to my ability to be loved”). Compassion towards the other means “you must have your painful reasons to do the things you are doing, and I am so sorry you are suffering.” I can treat everyone with respect. Treating people well is synonymous with handling things with grace. Revenge and hatred are extremely bitter and are shaped like boomerangs. Grace has an aftertaste like eucalyptus and honey, and is as light and replete as a breath. Finally, I take very good care of myself in the aftermath of the breakup. I make sure I am exercising and eating well. I prioritize sleep, even when I feel like I can’t. I need to show my nervous system that I’ve got me, in the middle of all this pain and this uncertainty. One day when I least expect it, I will find that I’ve come out of the worst time in my life smelling like roses. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can you tell real love from love bombing?
Answer: Love bombing is intense, exuberant, idealized, and has no boundaries. It wants things that normally take time to be instant: I love you. I want you all the time. We should get married. It’s so much so fast that it feels there is no room for anything else. Real love is not a roller coaster. It’s steady. It takes its time. It’s respectful. It’s boundaries. It’s a person focused on getting to know you rather than focused on getting you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Do you think loneliness is a personal choice?
Answer: Loneliness is dark, a vast emptiness, a sense of isolation, the belief that there is no one out there, that I am in this alone. It’s desolation. Solitude is being alone, in my own company. It’s fulfilling time, full time, peace time, my time, quiet time, time to process, time to rest, time to do things I like doing with myself. I don’t think loneliness is entirely related to being in the company of others: many people feel deeply lonely even when they have friends and family and people who love them. Loneliness is an internal affliction related to a sense of meaning and connection. I think solitude is a choice. Loneliness is not. Loneliness is inherent to the human condition, a constant or recurring shadow we cannot run from.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Does grief impact your ability to listen to people talk or even care what they are going through?
Answer: Imagine you are standing inside an elevator, talking to a friend. She is telling you about her life and you are interested and able to listen. Suddenly, the elevator starts filling with water. The water rises to your ankles, then your knees, then your hips. Your friend is still talking to you, and you feel the water rising to your belly button, to your chest. Of course grief impacts your ability to listen. Don't you see? You are drowning. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Did you change because you had to or you wanted to?
Answer: Living with high levels of anxiety and feeling resentful of people who were important to me became too painful to withstand. It was no way to live. I changed because I had to. Why did I perceive things the way that I did? Why did I do the things I did? Was there a way I could suffer less? Maybe if I shifted how I reacted to things, life could be less painful. Maybe if I could identify what it was that I needed to work on. I changed because I wanted to.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why is “I don’t love you anymore” always an excuse to break up? Is it a way for them to run away from the problems in front of them?
Answer: Relationships are voluntary. I am in one because I want to be. Each participant in a relationship is endowed with free will. As such, no one needs an excuse to break up. You can break up for a good reason, for a bad reason, or for no reason. “I don’t love you anymore” is a good reason to leave, but also a good reason to not want to stay.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: He says we rushed into things and he’s not ready for a relationship but he won’t break up with me. What do I do or how do I act?
Answer: These are strong statements! If he said we rushed into things, that he was not ready for a relationship, I’d be so wrapped up in that I would neglect to consider one thing. And, me? Setting him aside, how do I feel? Do I agree we rushed into things? Am I ready for a relationship? The answer to these questions lends me the clarity I need to decide what to do next. If we want similar things - to take it a bit slower, essentially, before fully committing to each other - I would recalibrate the time and emotional effort I am putting into the relationship and continue to explore it. If I feel ready for a relationship and he doesn’t, I would be the one to decide to break up. “I completely understand you feel rushed and not ready! To me, this means we want different things.” I am not a passive participant in deciding what to do next. It’s not just up to him. It’s also up to me, and hinges on wanting similar things for ourselves and our relationship.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Do you respect able bodied people who are in their 40's and have never moved out of their parent's home?
Answer: Whenever I meet someone and get to talk to them and listen I am struck by the complexity of their life. A person’s life looks something like this: When I interact with them, it’s just at a tiny intersection. What I see looks like this: Because I can see so little of a life so rich, because I lack the context to why they do what they do, I refrain from judging any of the choices they make. I mean, what the heck do I know?

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it wrong of me to ask my married, 40-year-old daughter why her and her husband decided not to have children? I fully respect the choice that they made, but I am curious why they chose not to.
Answer: This is tricky. Very tricky. “Why did you decide not to have children” is treacherous territory. It can be perceived as invasive, even disrespectful, hurtful. But, it’s not coming from a stranger. It’s coming from a mother. Here are the questions you need to ask yourself. (I am not asking so you can tell me. I am asking so you can self-reflect.) How is your relationship with your daughter? Supportive, loving, kind? Have you asked her many times when oh when they are finally going to give you grandchildren? Do you have a history of making her feel like you are meddling, or disrespecting boundaries? Are you invested in things going your way, rather than her way, when it comes to her life? Where is your question coming from? Just curiosity? Does it feel like “I just wanna know” or does it feel like “I love you, and I want you to feel you can talk to me?” Does it feel like “I will support you no matter what” or like “I want to get in there and attempt to change your mind”? Does it feel like “I want to hear about your life and the shape you dream it will take” or does it feel like “I want to know if I did something that would lead to you making this decision?” In other words, is this about her, or is this about you? If you are just curious, if you want to influence or criticize, if you want to get her to change her mind, if you cannot support what she and her husband have elected to do with their lives, then, yes. It’s wrong of you to ask. If you want a closer relationship with your daughter, if you just want to listen, if you are free of judgement, if you have no agenda, then ask her, but give her an out: “You don’t have to say a word. You don’t have anything to explain. I respect you and the choices that you make. I love you, and if you want to talk, I am right here.”

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you stop your emotions from dictating your actions?
Answer: Here are a few things that work for me: If I am feeling any strong emotion - anger, sadness, anxiety, frustration - I declare myself unable to make any decisions. I give myself a time out. During this time out, I move. A walk does wonders for me. Sometimes I need a double time out - I say something like “I need some time to process this so give me a few days and I will get back to you.” I do what I need to to get out of my emotions, out of my thoughts, and into my body. I jump up and down. I go to the freezer and hold ice in my hand. I smell essential oils. I find jumping into my body protects me from falling prey to clouded judgment. I put my emotion into words. Extra points if I can articulate emotional nuance. Something like: it’s not that I am angry. It’s that I feel hurt. I don’t feel betrayal but I do feel left out. I don’t feel jealous but I do feel disrespected. Knowing exactly how I feel helps me stand up for myself more clearly. I talk to myself. Dushka, what if the other person is doing the best they can? What if I am the one who is wrong? What if the other person is right? What if I could be seeing this differently? Is my emotion out of proportion with the situation? Is this me reacting from something that’s happened before? Am I somewhere in my past? What if there is more than one correct perspective? There is almost always more than one correct perspective. Can you find the one the other person is holding? I describe the situation from the point of view of the other person. This can be extremely hard, even painful, but it helps me be more centered, more understanding and maybe more empathetic. The exercise almost always calms me down.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it fair to say that 99% of people you meet in your life aren't worth a damn?
Answer: I went on a walk yesterday and came across a stranger and her dog. The dog saw me and acted like I was her long lost best friend so I asked if I could give the pup a generous amount of pets and sritchies. “Of course!” she said. “She would love that!” As I fussed over the pup, the woman told me she had only had her for a few months. “She belonged to a friend who died” she said. “I didn't want her dog to go through any more loss.” We stood there, two strangers, talking about life and the strange, unexpected turns it takes. How we move through it mostly clueless. How, if we are lucky, we cross paths with creatures who decide to love us. I’ve met people I adore and I’ve met people I don't like much. But I’ve never, ever come across someone who I’d classify as not worth a damn.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How hurt are you after you are unfriended?
Answer: Many years ago I had two friends who were a couple. They told my group of friends they were getting a divorce. Everyone in the group made an effort to stay in touch with both of them. Over time, the guy continued to reach out to us and spend time with us. She blocked all of us across social media. We were very sad that she did this, but also we understood. Getting over a divorce is hard, and sometimes you just need space. You feel like you need to start over. Even if being unfriended makes me feel a pang of sadness, I assume the person who did it has their reasons, and that most of them are not really about me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What makes someone say you are hard to read?
Answer: Imagine for a moment you are playing poker. You have an incredibly good hand and don’t want others to know. You are careful not to seem excited or overjoyed. You are guarded with your body language. You keep your expressions in check. If someone is hard to read, you look at them and are not quite sure what they are feeling or thinking. It’s the opposite of wearing your heart on your sleeve.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is telling someone, If they are busy or don’t have time to reply or even read your message, to NOT open your messages until they are not busy (or whatever) so they don’t leave you on seen because it makes you overthink, considered setting a boundary?
Answer: It is not. A boundary is an expression of my limits and is about me. Control is a demand on another person. We cannot ask other people to alter their behavior to accommodate our emotions. Regulating my emotions is on me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I set healthy boundaries without feeling guilty when I enforce them?
Answer: Sometimes I want a big bowl of crispy chips more than I want a salad. I want to sit on the couch more than I want to go out for a walk. I want to stay up late talking or watching a movie more than I want to go to bed early. Sometimes making the healthy choice feels uncomfortable, and making an unhealthy choice feels easier, more tempting, more fun. The same is true for boundaries. Setting them is good for me, healthy for me, and it will not feel comfortable. I will feel guilty or selfish or disloyal. And doing it will, over time, protect me from feeling overextended and resentful. (It will also protect others from the grumpiest version of me.) Over time, making healthy choices will get easier. A salad will in fact sound crunchier and fresher than chips. Going out for a walk will feel more mind clearing and breezier than the couch. And, going to bed early will feel downright delicious. The same is true for boundaries. They get easier over time. Over time, you realize. I should have been saying no all along.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What do you wish someone had told you about relationships in high school?
Answer: What I remember most about High School is the energy I expended to get others to like me, in particular if they seemed aloof or if they acted in a way that was not consistent. Inconsistency felt like such a rush. I can make you love me. I wish someone had told me that any form of chasing is ineffective. It doesn’t work but when it does you end up surrounded by people who are not really interested in you. I wish someone had said “be who you are and communicate as clearly as you can, and refrain from expending effort in influencing how others feel about you.” You are not supposed to “win people over.” Any form of a chase, any effort, any plot, any plan to “get someone to like me” will accomplish the opposite of what I want to find: someone as interested in me as I am in them.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do I feel the urge to do something, but don't know what?
Answer: To me, anxiety often presents itself as: The urge to do something, but I don’t know what. The sense that I am forgetting something. The feeling that nothing is in its place. What helps me is to recognize that the more I attempt to find what it is that I have the urge to do, the more it will elude me. The more I check what I could possibly be forgetting, the more I feel like there is something I am missing. The more I organize, the more I feel overcome by entropy. So, I switch. I take my anxiety for a walk outside. I put on a song I like and dance to it. I take a few long, deep breaths. I call a friend, ask how they are doing and really listen. All these things take me outside my brain and all the things she obsesses about that I can’t quite reach. Slowly, slowly, I recover the feeling that it’s possible there is nothing urgent I need to do. I am not forgetting anything, and if I am, I can recover from having forgotten it. And maybe, just maybe, everything is right where it's supposed to be. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I don't know what I like and what I don't like at all. It's not normal. I don’t mean like some things, I mean everything. Why?
Answer: Knowing what I like seems obvious but is really hard. This is because my brain plays tricks on me: If a lot of other people like something, my brain will tell me I like it too. Think of how many people get married and have kids without pausing to consider if that’s what they want. If I believe something is beyond my reach, my brain will convince me that I don’t like it. What if instead I told myself that even unattainable things are worth the effort? Where would that take me? If I don’t like something but feel I need to accommodate it, I will tell myself that what I don’t like “is not so bad”. This is how we get stuck for years in empty relationships and unsatisfying jobs. If something is forbidden, my brain thinks I really want it (when I’m just attracted to it because I can’t have it.) Think of how many teenagers end up in the arms of the person their parents told them they were not allowed to spend time with. If I am afraid to like what I like - if I believe it means people will not approve of me, will not support me, if I think it will isolate me - then I don’t really know how to like it. Think about the artist in a family of scientists. If I am in a state of flux (and, we are always in a state of flux) I might truly like something one day, and not like it in the future. As I change, I have to get to know me over and over. I thought I didn’t like Brussels sprouts. I thought I liked beach vacations. I didn’t know I was a city person. Knowing what I like is hard, and as such not knowing is normal. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What's the difference between telling someone what to do and inspiring them to do it themselves?
Answer: Telling someone what to do is easy. It makes me feel useful, helpful, like I am solving something - it makes me feel worthy. And yet, it is presumptuous, inappropriate, disrespectful and invasive. Instead, I need to assume what the other person deserves: that they are capable. Also - and this is the crux of the matter - telling another person what to do with their life and their decisions distracts me from what I need to do with my life and my decisions. The work that I need to do never ends. Do I love myself? Do I believe in myself? Do I take responsibility? What do I stand for? Do I act with courage? Do I speak up when I need to? Am I setting healthy boundaries? Do I have compassion, for myself and for others? Am I kind? Do I communicate with clarity, with empathy? Telling someone what to do is irritating, meddlesome, and contemptuous. Loving myself enough to want to be a better person is inspiring.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are the benefits of saying “no” without having to explain yourself?
Answer: Feeling like I have to explain myself is a lot of work. It’s energy. It’s a form of control. It’s people pleasing: feeling like I need to get others to agree with me, to approve of me, or to not feel hurt about a choice I am making. To accomplish this, I give long answers, share more information than I need to, and then wonder why I said so much. The truth is this: I can make decisions that are right for me without seeking approval. I am not responsible for keeping track of or maintaining how other people feel. Instead of saying - “I am so sorry I can’t come to your party! I haven’t been feeling well and have so much work to catch up on but also I have plans with friends from out of town so maybe we can stop by but I don’t know if…” I can just say - “your party sounds like so much fun. I’m sorry I can’t make it.” The benefits are less effort, less strain, more honesty, clean communication, clear boundaries and freedom from feeling like I need to control how everyone feels to make a little bit of room for what I desperately need.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why is giving advice that no one asked for considered rude?
Answer: Because, if you give me unsolicited advice, you’re assuming you know better than I do what I need to do about something related to me and not you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why does someone tell me they are sad but don’t want to tell me why?
Answer: Sometimes I let someone know I am sad to give my sadness a bit of space; and because this way I don’t have to hide how I really feel. Saying “I am sad” puts an end to all the pretending. “I am sad” means “I want you to know how I feel” but it can also mean “I don’t feel like going out” or “I don’t feel like talking” or “I don’t feel peppy, chatty or like I can be much fun.” Sometimes I don’t tell people why I am sad because I am not ready to talk about it, because it’s due to something private, or because I have not articulated it and don’t know yet why I feel this way. I think knowing how people around us feel gives us a window into why they behave the way they do, which fosters tolerance, intimacy and understanding. We are under no obligation to explain or justify our feelings if we don’t want to or are not ready.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do I feel I’m suffocating all the time?
Answer: Feeling like I cannot get enough air in my lungs is so awful and so scary. When I feel like I am suffocating the anxiety of being unable to breathe often makes my breathing even worse. Without context, without any sense for your lifestyle or medical history, no one has any way of knowing why you feel like you are suffocating. Here are just a few wide ranging possible reasons that are not exclusive: You are anxious You are unsafe and feel threatened You are in a relationship with someone extremely controlling You don’t set good boundaries and feel deeply resentful You feel the burden of unreasonable expectations You feel manipulated You do not have or cannot get to your own space: you have no personal time You cannot recharge You have no privacy You are feeling unheard, lied to or gaslighted You cannot express yourself You are in a situation you feel you cannot change You are being monitored You are being blackmailed You have low blood pressure You have asthma You are sick and have something in your lungs, such as pneumonia or even a cold You have a heart condition You have allergies You are in a room set at a high temperature The weather is extremely hot You are at high altitude You exercise extremely strenuously You should not feel like you are suffocating. Please see a doctor. If aside from feeling suffocated you feel faint, you feel pain in your chest, our if your lips look blue, please go to the emergency room.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: If the mind is not aware of an object does this object exist?
Answer: Every time I drive a car I remind myself that they are areas I cannot see, even when I look into all my mirrors. If another car approaches fast on the back left or the back right side of the car, my mind might not be aware of their existence. My lack of awareness does not mean they don't exist: my awareness does not determine an object’s existence. Many, many things exist, even if I don’t see them, know about them or believe in them.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: People I consider my friends didn't say happy birthday to me but people I haven't talked to in years have. What should I do?
Answer: To suffer less, I would: Notice when I am expecting people to “just know” what I want, and stop doing that. People should not have to read my mind. I cannot demand something impossible and then be disappointed when it doesn’t take place. Asking my friends if I can send them a “repeats once a year” calendar notification so that they remember my birthday. Throw myself a birthday party every year and saying “please bring birthday wishes and a card. Observing my birthday is important to me.” Note my birthday on my social media channel of choice so that people I don’t talk to much can remember my birthday too. Most importantly, I need to stop measuring friendship in relation to who remembers my birthday. It’s a nice, thoughtful gesture, but I can also have deep, true, meaningful relationships with people who have no idea what day I was born.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do some people reject compliments?
Answer: Because, a compliment makes me feel exposed. Because it’s unexpected and as such makes me feel like I am not in control. Because what you are saying and what I believe are causing cognitive dissonance and I need time to reconcile the two. Because, I’m afraid I’ve somehow set high expectations and will end up disappointing you. Because it feels like if I accept the compliment it will make me come across as too full of myself. Related:

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What's the difference between honest and sincere?
Answer: They are near-synonymous. If I am being honest, I am being upright, truthful, fair. Something sincere is pure and contains nothing false. I can give you a sincere compliment, a sincere apology.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Would you prefer someone kind or honest?
Answer: This question is a false dichotomy and assumes that to be kind you have to sacrifice the truth. It means being with people who feel they have to manage reality for me. I prefer those who refrain from compromising on either one.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Should you wish someone happy birthday if they haven't wished you a happy birthday?
Answer: To me, keeping score feels constraining and narrow and tight. It means I keep track of the times I have been disappointed, give only when the giving comes with things I expect to get in return. The calculations burden me. I don’t think they are good for me, or for my relationships. What I want instead is to give because it makes me happy. Because giving without expectations frees me from resentment and bitterness. I want to appreciate the fact that people express love in different ways. I have a friend who never remembers my birthday, but always makes me feel heard. Eliminating quid pro quo dynamics is one of the big gifts that comes from learning how to set boundaries. I protect myself from one-sided relationships, from feeling taken advantage of, and from that clear place I can be as generous as I want, without compromising myself and without ever needing to keep score.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why do I always end up with the guys that take advantage of me when I’m so kind?
Answer: Feeling like I am being taken advantage of is such an awful, sad, isolating, hopeless feeling. To protect myself from it, I am very careful to make a clean, clear distinction between kindness and poor boundaries. Being helpful, loving and generous of spirit never compromises me. It enriches me. Poor boundaries mean I overextend myself, have trouble saying no, do things for others at the cost of my own peace of mind. Clear boundaries put me in a place where I can be kind, but where others cannot take advantage of me. This makes my relationships better too because boundaries protect others from my own feelings of bitterness and resentment.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I'm constantly underestimated by others. Why is this so? What does this signify?
Answer: Where is the emotion that you are looking to understand? Is it in you, or is it in another? If you are being underestimated, the people doing the underestimating are others, not you. I am pointing this out because we are not responsible for the emotions of others. We can only be responsible for our own emotions. What this means is that we can’t change them or fix them. Why do people underestimate others? For reasons related to themselves, not to you. People underestimate because of ignorance, because of prejudice, because of insecurity, because they project onto another person how they feel about themselves. Because conceiving of others as small or weak grants us the illusion of strength. What can you do about this? I will share with you what my father told me many years ago when I lamented I was being underestimated. “But Dushka” he said. “Being underestimated is the single greatest strategic advantage.” So, tell me. Now that you know you are at a strategic advantage, what will you do with it? (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Does making a girl jealous make her want you more?
Answer: There are many, many different kinds of people out there so of course, making some women jealous makes them want you more. If someone deliberately attempted to make me jealous I’d feel at a loss; perplexed rather than wanting. The kind of relationship I seek is the one that makes me feel safe rather than threatened. I want a life of harmony and peace. Playing games that manipulate my vulnerability is not interesting to me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is there a such thing as an introvert who doesn’t mind engaging in conversation with people they don’t know everywhere they go ?
Answer: What defines an introvert happens after they engage in conversation with people they don’t know everywhere they go. Are they charged or depleted by the interactions? If they feel charged by social interaction they are extroverted. If they feel depleted by the interaction, even if they enjoy the interaction while it happens, then they are introverted. What defines an introvert is where their energy comes from, rather than their interest or ability to socialize. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the difference between “jealous” and “petty”?
Answer: Jealous: I feel like someone can take away the person that I love. Petty: narrow minded, lacking generosity of spirit, being small-natured.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I want my husband and I to have our own separate bedrooms when I get married. Is it okay and is it not embarrassing?
Answer: You don’t ever need to do anything the way “other people” do things. You can find your own way of doing them. What you decide to do should be determined by your own needs, by your own wants, not on how “other people” might react to what you do. (Obvious exception: unless what you are doing harms others, is illegal or boundary breaking.) “Other people” will always talk about how you do things, in particular if you do things differently. Pay no mind. Pay no mind because you will forever be judged no matter what you decide to do. You might as well do you. If you want to have separate bedrooms after you get married, two people need to agree on this decision, and two people only: your husband, and you.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some examples of a person letting their ego get in the way?
Answer: Examples of ego getting in the way: If someone says I hurt their feelings and I say “you are being sensitive”, because I can’t make space for possibly being wrong. If someone attempts to give me feedback and I interpret it as an attack. If someone is in a bad mood and I assume it’s because of me. If I’m playing a game with friends and I lose and get angry. Fighting to win instead of fighting to understand. Needing to be right, more than learning how to listen. Feeling like I always want more, in a way that makes me unable to appreciate what I have. Feeling like I need to know everything rather than being open to learning something new. Really needing help and being unable to ask for it. Feeling like I need to control everything. Losing interest if I am not the center of attention. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: If me and my partner has a completely different mindset, beliefs, and thinking, is this relationship still going to work in the long run, or should I still stay?
Answer: It’s possible for two people to love each other a lot and have different mindsets, beliefs and thinking and decide, based on their differences, to part ways. The reasons for things to unfold in this way are twofold: beliefs that are not just different and incompatible; and/or an inability to communicate with clarity and respect. It’s also possible for two people to have very different mindsets, beliefs and thinking and create a rich relationship that widens their perspective on life. The requirements for this to happen are twofold: very good communication, and very different yet compatible thinking.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What’s the point of putting effort forward if I might fail and won’t be appreciated for my hard work and be rewarded for my efforts?
Answer: Effort teaches me about myself. Do I put in the work? What do I value? What motivates me? Do I get in my own way, convince myself that what I want is not worth fighting for? Through effort I show myself that I am capable of much more than I initially gave myself credit for. The reward is confidence and self-esteem, regardless of the outcome. Effort is how I work through fear. Every day I try, and every day I show myself what I can do. In incremental steps I make fear smaller. Through effort I don't just learn new things - I realize I can learn new things. My learning becomes exponential. Effort teaches me about adaptation. How much am I getting ahead with X amount of work? What do I need to be doing differently? Effort teaches me about concentration and focus: it’s an antidote to distraction and procrastination. Of course it’s possible to put a lot of effort into something and fail or go unnoticed. But effort changes my regard for myself, diminishes self-doubt and builds character. And that’s the point of effort.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Should I wait for her? She said she wants me but wants me to wait. What should I do?
Answer: How do you feel when you really like someone? I feel giddy. I feel excited. I feel lucky. I feel I want to spend time with them and get to know them. If someone says “I want you, but I want you to wait” they may want me, but they don’t want me in the way I want them, and as such I consider them not compatible with me. I want someone who feels giddy, excited and lucky, and who wants to spend time with me and get to know me. If that’s not how they are, I understand that. But they are not for me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is it true that I don't need to seek people's acceptance? How will people accept me?
Answer: If I do anything that feels like chasing, like convincing, like “making” someone accept or like me, if there is any plotting in me “showing” you that I am worth your time and attention, the result will be forced, anxious, inconsistent. I will end up in one-sided relationships, or with people who are not really available, who do not feel about me the way I feel about them. Instead, I need to trust: trust that I am worth loving. To focus on getting to know myself and being true to that. No effort to get you to like me, but rather full transparency: “this is who I am” and “this is what I need” even if I am afraid to disappoint or burden you. I believe that you and I deserve to be loved, accepted and approved of for who we are. Also, I am not for everyone, so some people will accept me and some won’t. The people I care about who care about me in return - the real me, not the struggling to get your approval me - are my people.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Do you experience intuition as a feeling, or instead as a thought or mental picture?
Answer: I experience intuition as a feeling that has no pictures and no words. She presents herself in the form of a knot, a pang, a pit in my gut, a flash of clarity, a burst of light inside my chest, an inner flare. Often, the feeling is followed by a command. For example, I feel a pit in my gut, then a “no!” I trust my intuition to keep me safe, to tell me when something is off, and in particular, I trust her in matters of love. Time has proven she has good taste in men. I do not feel like my intuition is “always right”. I don’t think there is anything about humans that is perfectly infallible. She doesn’t have to always be right for me to know she’s worth listening to.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What is the worst thing people say to you when you are going through a hard time?
Answer: I told you so. You are not given anything you cannot handle. So many people have it so much worse. You are so lucky. I feel sorry for you. Chin up. Snap out of it. How did you get yourself into this? Be grateful. Everything happens for a reason.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What's the difference between why and how?
Answer: There is a very famous story about a group of mice who keep getting attacked by a cat. They all get together to attempt to solve this. “We need to do something to stop these attacks! We want to live!” (This is the “why”: it’s purpose, motivation, what drives us.) “Why don’t we put a bell on the cat, so we can hear it coming towards us?” Says one of the mice. Everyone agrees this is a brilliant, excellent idea. “But wait”, asks one mouse. “Who will put the bell on the cat?” (This is “how”.)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My son lost his first tooth and my husband threw it away while I was at work. Am I wrong for getting so angry at my husband that I ignored him for the rest of the day?
Answer: Relationships are really frightening. They expose me, and I spend most of my time assessing if I am safe or if I am in danger. Feeling safe makes my relationship more solid. I’ve got you. We are in this together. We are a team. We can figure this out. Feeling like I am in danger weakens it, because I begin to protect myself from it, become distant, become doubtful, become defensive. Examples of things that weaken my relationship, maybe not instantly but certainly over time, are things like the silent treatment or ignoring someone. You are not worth a conversation, I am saying. When things get tough, you don’t even deserve my attention. Of course you are “right” to be angry. You might begin by saying “I am so furious about this I am going to take a bit of time to process what happened, so we can talk about it. Please give me a few days.” Once you are ready, you can say “you throwing away something deeply meaningful to me, something that cannot be replaced, hurt me very much.” Then you can talk about it, and perhaps understand the reason why he did what he did. There is always room for more than one “correct” perspective. A fight is meant for us to understand each other better. It’s meant to stand as proof that my commitment to you will not falter, even if I am angry (unless what you do is a dealbreaker). It’s meant to say “our relationship can withstand storms and become steadier.” Whenever I feel overcome by emotion I ask myself - how can I handle this so that the person that I love does not feel unsafe? Because an absence of safety has a price, and over time it will cost me the relationship.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why should people accept their age?
Answer: Because resisting something immutable is exhausting and accomplishes nothing. Because spinning up anxiety and distress over something I have no power over is a waste of energy I could be using for less futile things. Because wishing things were different is a battle against reality and a battle against reality is me being locked into something I can never win (or even budge.) Because believing I can go back to the way things were will keep me stuck. Pushing against reality will make me angry, frustrated, bitter, tense, stressed, hopeless and depressed. Refusing to accept is resistance and resistance will distract me from figuring out how to make the best of what I have.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What do I do when a friend I have wants to know everything I do?
Answer: If I have a friend who wants to know everything I do I set a boundary. “Hey, I like you and appreciate our friendship, but you want to know everything I do and I don’t want to share everything I do. Here is what I am comfortable talking about. Here is what I am not comfortable talking about.” I don’t need to explain my boundaries, but if I wanted to I could say “this has nothing to do with secrecy. It has to do with privacy, and the fact that there are some things I am not comfortable sharing.”

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: When a friend constantly has an attitude towards you, do you need better friends?
Answer: If a friend constantly has an attitude towards me, I would talk to her. I would carefully define what I mean by “attitude” to articulate my interpretation of what she is doing, I would explain how it makes me feel, and then I would listen. There are always many sides to a story. It’s possible for us to have very different perspectives and both be right (or wrong.) But mostly, friends are worth getting ourselves through difficult periods of our friendship. I want to learn to overcome uncomfortable things by talking through them and being open to other versions of what I experience, rather than just leave when things get uncomfortable. This to grow and become more self-aware, and to avoid a pattern where I leave when things get hard, only to witness the same problems arising over and over across all my relationships. Of course there comes a time when the dynamic has run its course. But, not without knowing that I made an effort to preserve my friendship. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Does someone really suffer when we wish bad for them?
Answer: Absolutely. If I wish someone ill, I spin up a lot of energy inside of me filled with anger, with hatred, with bitterness. I keep the person at the center of my attention. When I wish someone ill, I both create and perpetuate a cycle of hurt that places me at the center of it, like being followed by a dark storm of my own doing. If I wish someone ill, the person who suffers is me.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How long is an eternity?
Answer: When I was a kid I was reading a mystery novel that included a quote by someone else with an explanation intended to help me grasp the definition of eternity. It went something like this: Imagine an enormous granite mountain twice as high as Mount Everest. Once every thousand years, a bird flies by and lightly grazes the top of the mountain with its wing. The time it takes for the mountain to become a grain of sand due to the friction caused by the bird’s wing is only a fraction of a second in the context of eternity. I don’t know who originally explained eternity like this but it stuck in my mind and it's what I think about every time I hear the word.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: I made a dozen cupcakes as a gift to a friend. When I handed them to her, she started offering them to everyone around her. In the end, she had about 5 left. Would you be offended?
Answer: The wife of a good friend of mine gave him a watch. She put time and effort into finding the right one for him, spent quite a bit of money on it and presented it with flourish. He loved it and put it on immediately. A couple of weeks later we were all at dinner and my friend’s best friend noticed the new watch on his wrist. “Wow” he said. “That is a gorgeous time piece you’ve got there.” My friend immediately took it off and handed it over. “If you like it, you should have it.” My friend’s wife was furious. How could he give away her gift? How could he be so thoughtless? He looked shocked. “But, if you give me something, it belongs to me, which means I am free to do with it whatever I want.” The incident was dismissed by them both. I think that technically my friend was right - the watch was his, for him to wear or give away. But, it doesn’t matter, since his wife has feelings, and her feelings are worth accounting for. I wish she had made space for what she was feeling, said something like “even if the watch belongs to you, it makes me feel that I am not important to you if you give away something I’ve given you.” I wish he had made space for her feelings, said something like “I gave the watch away because I love it, not because I don’t, and I am so very sorry that hurt you.” Which is to say, no matter what we think about what we feel, no matter what anyone thinks about how we feel, our feelings are here to tell us something. I think it’s important to pay them attention, and address them with the reverence that they deserve.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Why is effort important?
Answer: How can you get where you want to go? How can you become really good at something? How can you learn something new? The answer to all three questions is effort. But, perhaps more importantly, effort is also the answer to finding a sense of purpose, to feeling proud, to developing confidence, to building character, to arriving at the end of the day feeling satisfied with what you’ve done. Effort is important because it’s key to feeling fulfilled.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: The Mind: Why do I make up conversations in my head and sometimes I even find myself saying them out loud?
Answer: I make up conversations in my head and I think it’s a request (compulsion?) coming from my anxiety. Maybe if we can anticipate it, maybe if we can plan for it, maybe if we play out different scenarios, we will be prepared. We will be less surprised. We will be more in control. The problem is this: my anxiety lies to me (she’s not deceitful. She is just afraid.) I cannot possibly anticipate every possible scenario (but can overwhelm myself trying.) And, the conversations and what people say are not a reflection of others, but a reflection of me and what I am afraid they are going to do. I end up stressing myself, rather than preparing myself. What helps is for me to find a distraction. The one most effective for me is to listen to something: a podcast, a meditation, a story, an audiobook. It’s more useful, I think, to learn something new or to take a few deep breaths than to spin myself up over things that have never taken place.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: When a therapist wants me to ‘process’ something, what does that actually mean? What does processing something look and feel like?
Answer: When I was in my early twenties my boyfriend and I were emptying out the dishwasher and he dropped and shattered plate I loved. I felt fury. In tears, I accused him of being careless with my things. Throughout the day, I felt, more or less in order: Wrath. Sadness. A sort of grief, a disquiet, disproportionate to what actually took place. Then, I remembered that if I broke something when I was a kid, the reaction was similar to the one I had displayed with my boyfriend. This caused me to overreact, and treat him unfairly. I apologized. A few months ago, I was emptying out the dishwasher and accidentally slammed a bowl against the counter and broke it. I sat in my kitchen looking at the crack and took a deep breath. This is just a bowl. Breaking it was just an accident. I felt a touch of chagrin, then threw it in the trash and got on with my day. This is processing - a sort of mental and emotional sorting that, given the time and the space, happens without my direct intervention. On the other side of it we receive the gift of integration, which results in different, less painful reactions to similar things.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Am I so introverted if I feel tired of a 1-hour conversation?
Answer: I have a friend I can talk to for a whole afternoon. After we hang out I go home and feel socially drained, but also inspired. My brain feels sprinkled with stardust. There are other people I talk to for an hour or less who leave me feeling completely wiped out. This might be because they are belligerent, or hostile, or rambling, or complaining, or demanding, or talking at me and not really to me. It might be because I feel emotionally dumped on, because it feels like they want to talk, but not really talk to me. It might be because there is something about the interaction that I can’t reconcile, something that doesn’t quite add up that my brain keeps trying to make sense of. It might just be incompatible energies, or I don’t know what, but I go home after and feel like I need days to recover from the interaction. Later, I see their name on my phone and feel dread. I trust this feeling, and protect myself and my energy from people who seem to have this depleting effect on me. As an introvert, being social always takes a toll. Except, my experience depends not just on the fact that I am introverted, but on who I am spending time with.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What are some tips to go from being a "thinker" to being more of a "doer"?
Answer: I could give you a handful of relevant, even inspiring tips, like: If “the right time” does not exist, then the right time is now. Forget about getting things perfect. Perfect will get you stuck. Forget about eliminating risk. Life is risk. Motivation does not strike on its own. It’s action that begets motivation. And one I find really useful: take what you want to do, break it into small steps and commit to doing it 10 minutes a day. But really, the only way to go from thinking to doing is to stop reading “how to do” lists, get up and start. Go.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What do you write in a card for someone going through a difficult time?
Answer: Whenever I am writing a card for someone going through a difficult time, I remind them all of the difficult things they did not think they could get through, but did. I think we ourselves are the proof we need of our own resilience.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: What's the difference between 'I was right' and 'I guessed correctly'?
Answer: To me, the difference is attribution. “I was right” means I did the right thing, or I was correct, or I what I did was justified. The credit is mine. “I guessed correctly” is something like “I did not have enough evidence but managed to estimate accurately”. It’s not that I knew. It’s that I was lucky.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: My fiance passed away recently. How do I know if he is okay?
Answer: My dad died a decade ago and I often ask myself this question. The truth is no one knows, which means my own answer holds as much authority as any answer. This is what I do. I sit somewhere quiet and think of him. What was he like? What was our relationship like? How has my view on events shifted over time? What would he want to know, if he were to arrive and needed an update of what he’s missed? What would be find alarming (a lot) or funny (a lot)? Then I wait and see how this lands inside of me. Here is what I feel: That he is doing well. That he is not far away. That he is able to regard things with a broader perspective than the one he had when I knew him and as such he worries less and smiles more, often wryly. And, regarding any update I can give him: he already knows.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do you choose to be happy not because everything is perfect, but because you chose to focus on the perfect moments?
Answer: I agree that sometimes happiness is a matter of shifting my focus. But this strategy can come very close to denial, to shutting down something within me that’s trying to tell me something. It’s turning away from discomfort and distress when all emotions - every one - need attention and care. I can’t be happy all of the time. Things disquiet me, affect me, sadden me. What works for me is to sit with these feelings, feel them, breathe them in, acknowledge their right to be present in my life. It’s not that you have some kind of faulty perspective, Dushka. It’s not a matter of “choosing” to focus on something else. It’s that not every feeling is a “happy” feeling, but every feeling has a right to be here and giving it space and time, well. That’s how you choose to be happy. (Drawing by Dan Roam)

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How can you accept things you don't like, but you have no choice and must accept it?
Answer: I don’t think accepting is something I actively do. It’s not an action. It’s more like leaving the door ajar. I follow a series of steps to allow acceptance to show up and step inside on her own. Here are the steps: Do you know what I do when I don’t like the way things are? I resist. Resistance feels like tension, frustration, exasperation; like swimming against the current, like anger, like overwhelm. It drains me. I am getting better at identifying this resistance and when I do I name it. “Oh. This is me, resisting something I can’t change.” I don’t say “this is terrible or awful or futile or brave”. I just notice it. I try to articulate where my feeling is. For example - are my shoulders scrunched? Is my jaw locked? Is my breath tight? I address the feeling in my body by relaxing, unclenching, loosening the place affected by the resistance. It’s shocking to witness how much this helps. Then, I shift my energy somewhere else. I can got on a walk or straighten out a drawer or fold my laundry or water my plants or call a friend or get to work. Shifting my energy away from what I can’t change is a step on the road to accepting. After some time (sometimes not too long, sometimes longer) I realize my resistance has faded. Hello, acceptance! Thank you for coming! Please. Come in.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: How do I get to focus on one thing when I am interested in everything?
Answer: Have you ever heard of the term “Renaissance man?” (or the more modern “Renaissance person”?) It refers to someone who knows a lot and is adroit at a broad range of things: someone with imagination, with style, well read, well educated, sophisticated. You go with this person to a party and they are charming, can talk to anyone about pretty much anything, are well dressed, are good dancers, speak multiple languages, are versed at things that surprise you. They can ice-skate, for example, or fly a plane, or are really good at playing backgammon. People who focus on one thing are fabulous: they are specialists. People who are interested in everything are also fabulous. They pick up a lot of different things and given the time become a Renaissance person.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: Is cutting down distractions the key to productivity?
Answer: To be at my most productive, I need focus but also need idle time. When I am working I feel like I’m squeezing my brain, wringing her out, after which she needs time to do nothing so she can recover her original fluffy shape. I can push myself and cut down distractions and demand more and refuse to get the rest and space I need but if I do these things they catch up to me in the form of listlessness, then burnout. Distractions are good because I feel better when I don’t treat myself like a machine.

Name: Dushka Zapata
Question: The best of you are the boundaries you put in your life. Is it correct?
Answer: Poor boundaries mean I feel taken advantage of. Like I say “yes” at my own expense. Like I try to meet everyone’s needs, but no one tries to meet mine. Boundaries are guardians, sentinels that protect the best parts of me from attack, from invasion, from annoyance and from resentment. The best of you is firmly, securely defended by the boundaries you create.
